title: Repurposing amlodipine, fluoxetine, and escitalopram as non-antibiotic adjuvants: in vitro enhancement of ciprofloxacin and fluconazole activity against multidrug-resistant bacterial and candida clinical isolates.
authors: Alkhawlani MA; Al-Madhagi WM; Alburyhi MM; Al-Kaf AG; Al-Najar M
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Candida albicans threaten treatment success, particularly in resource-limited settings. Repurposing licensed, inexpensive non-antibiotic drugs may provide a strategy for enhancing the activity of established antimicrobial agents.

METHODS: Clinical isolates from Sana'a, Yemen, and American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) reference strains were tested in vitro with amlodipine, fluoxetine, and escitalopram, individually and in dual or triple combinations with ciprofloxacin or fluconazole. Antimicrobial activity was evaluated using agar-well diffusion, broth microdilution minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), minimum bactericidal or fungicidal concentration (MBC/MFC), and checkerboard fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) assays. Molecular docking with AutoDock Vina was used to explore plausible interactions with MurB (PDB 1HSK), LasR (PDB 3IX3), and CYP51 (PDB 5V5Z). Normal mode analysis (NMA) with iMODS was performed for selected fluoxetine-LasR and fluoxetine-MurB complexes as a preliminary structural-dynamics assessment.

RESULTS: Fluoxetine produced inhibition zones of at least 27 mm across the tested organisms. Amlodipine produced larger zones against S. aureus and C. albicans than against P. aeruginosa, whereas escitalopram produced smaller zones overall. Checkerboard testing identified synergy (FICI ≤ 0.50) for selected combinations. Selected triple combinations reduced MIC values by 4- to 64-fold. The largest diffusion readouts were observed with ciprofloxacin + fluoxetine + amlodipine against S. aureus (101 mm), ciprofloxacin + fluoxetine + escitalopram against P. aeruginosa (88.5 mm), and ciprofloxacin + amlodipine + fluconazole against C. albicans (138.5 mm). Docking scores and NMA outputs provided hypothesis-generating structural context for the experimental findings.

CONCLUSIONS: Antimicrobial enhancement was combination- and organism-dependent. Selected combinations showed checkerboard-defined synergy, whereas diffusion assays were interpreted as screening outcomes only. Docking and NMA findings were supportive and hypothesis-generating but did not establish target engagement or mechanism.

title: Stk1 is required for BlaR1-mediated broad-spectrum β-lactam resistance in epidemic-causing strains of Staphylococcus aureus.
authors: Poon R; Satishkumar N; Mosimann WA; Hayatnagarkar VD; Bose S; Hemmadi V; Kuhn S; Chatterjee A; Worrall L; Manes NP; Alexander JAN; Lack J; Chambers HF; Nita-Lazar A; Strynadka NCJ; Chatterjee SS
abstract: Sensory induction of mecA expression plays a pivotal role in mediating broad-spectrum β-lactam resistance of MRSA. In contemporary MRSA isolates, sensory induction of β-lactam resistance originates at the membrane-associated BlaR1, which, upon detection of β-lactam drugs, triggers a signal transduction cascade that promotes mecA induction. We hereby show that phosphorylation of BlaR1, mediated through the serine-threonine kinase, Stk1, stabilizes its membrane-spanning state and retention, allowing for proper drug sensing and subsequent signal transduction events to occur, culminating in mecA-mediated β-lactam resistance. Our results demonstrate that targeting Stk1 can potentiate synthetic lethality to β-lactams in the majority of naturally isolated strains of MRSA. We additionally present the structural and kinetic basis for a Stk1-inhibitor complex that can enable rational design of Stk1-directed anti-MRSA therapeutics in the future. Our results reveal a novel role of the STK signaling pathway in bacterial protein stabilization in the cytosolic membrane.

title: In vitro Combinatorial Effects of 18β-Glycyrrhetinic Acid with Azole Antifungals.
authors: Zeng Y; Hu J; Ge L; Yu J; Tang M; Tan J; Zhang H; Sun Y
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To explore the combined effects of multiple drugs and provide more therapeutic options for invasive fungal infections, this study evaluated the in vitro susceptibility of Aspergillus spp. Candida spp. Cryptococcus neoformans, and Exophiala dermatitidis to 18β-glycyrrhetinic acid(GA) in combination with itraconazole(ITC), voriconazole(VRC), posaconazole(POS), and fluconazole(FLU).

METHODS: The antifungal activity of GA combined with ITC, VRC, POS, and FLU against 107 clinical isolates was evaluated using the CLSI broth microdilution method (M27-A3 and M38-A2), including 56 strains of Aspergillus spp. 16 strains of E. dermatitidis, 26 strains of Candida spp. and 9 strains of C. neoformans. Minimum inhibitory concentrations(MICs) and fractional inhibitory concentration indices(FICIs) were determined to evaluate the synergistic effects.

RESULTS: GA alone exhibited no antifungal activity. However, its combination with azoles showed complex biphasic effects. The synergistic rates of GA-POS against Aspergillus spp. E. dermatitidis, Candida spp. and C. neoformans were 87.50%(49/56), 43.75%(7/16), 30.77%(8/26), and 55.56%(5/9), respectively, with no antagonism observed, indicating broad-spectrum synergistic potential. In contrast, the synergistic rates of GA-ITC against the above pathogens were only 5.36%(3/56), 6.25%(1/16), 26.92%(7/26), and 22.22%(2/9), respectively. GA-FLU exerted synergistic effects only against C. neoformans(11.11%, 1/9). The overall synergistic rate ranked POS(64.49%, 69/107) > ITC(12.15%, 13/107) > FLU(4.00%, 1/25). Additionally, partial antagonistic effects were observed in Candida spp. and C. neoformans. For Candida spp. the antagonistic rates of GA-VRC and GA-FLU were 23.08%(6/26) and 25.00%(4/16), respectively. For C. neoformans, the antagonistic rate of GA-FLU was 22.22%(2/9).

CONCLUSION: In vitro experiments demonstrate that synergistic or antagonistic effects can be observed when GA is combined with azoles. These findings deepen our understanding of the combinatorial efficacy of GA and azoles and provide new perspectives for targeted antifungal combination therapy.

title: Vaginal Lactobacillus paragasseri may attenuate fluconazole-resistant phenotypes in the subset of Candida albicans isolates and shows potential as a probiotic adjunct in antifungal therapy.
authors: Wang Q; Wang H; Pan H; Xu Z; Cui Q; Zhao H; Jia K; Wang F
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Candida albicans is the predominant etiological agent of vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC). Fluconazole (FLU), a first-line azole antifungal agent, has encountered growing resistance among vaginal isolates of C. albicans due to prolonged, high-dose clinical administration. The development of such drug resistance arises from the synergistic interplay of multiple factors, with key mechanisms including enhanced biofilm formation, overexpression of drug efflux pump genes, and structural alterations in target enzymes driven by mutations in the ERG11 gene. Lactobacilli, the dominant commensal probiotics in the vaginal microbiota, are known to inhibit biofilm formation by C. albicans, a process closely linked to the development of antifungal resistance. Consequently, vaginal lactobacilli may serve as a pharmacological adjuvant to enhance the antifungal efficacy of fluconazole against C. albicans. While existing research has primarily focused on the inhibitory effects of Lactobacilli on C. albicans proliferation, investigations into their impact on antifungal resistance remain limited.

METHODS: We investigate the impact of vaginal L. paragasseri on fluconazole-resistance phenotypes in a subset of clinical fluconazole-resistant C. albicans isolates. Guided by established fluconazole-resistance mechanisms, we first screened fluconazole resistant C. albicans isolates by assessing biofilm formation capacity, drug efflux pump gene expression, and ERG11 gene mutations and mRNA expression. Next, analysis of the vaginal Lactobacillus composition in VVC patients and healthy controls showed a nominal, non-significant trend toward lower L. paragasseri detection in VVC-affected women. Motivated by this trend and by prior evidence that Lactobacilli can modulate antifungal-resistance phenotypes, we examined whether L. paragasseri modulates fluconazole-resistance in clinically derived C. albicans isolates through functional assays. Subsequent functional assessments, including standard antifungal susceptibility testing, biofilm formation assays, and drug efflux pump gene expression analyses.

RESULTS: Vaginal L. paragasseri can attenuate fluconazole-resistant phenotypes in the tested subset of clinical fluconazole-resistant C. albicans isolates. In a murine vulvovaginal candidiasis model, adjunctive treatment with L. paragasseri provided adjuvant benefit when added to fluconazole therapy, reducing vaginal C. albicans colonization and alleviating infection-associated tissue damage. These in-vivo observations constitute preliminary pre-clinical evidence.

DISCUSSION: These findings demonstrate that vaginal L. paragasseri holds promising potential as a probiotic adjunctive therapy for C. albicans-induced VVC, offering novel insights for the development of alternative antifungal therapeutic strategies.

title: A phytochemical-nanotechnology platform exhibits complementary antimicrobial and immunomodulatory effects in experimental fowl typhoid.
authors: Saleem A; Farhat B; Mir Y; Manzoor T; Nazir J; Ahmad SF; Ganai AM; Attia SM; Prasad M; Ahmad SM
abstract: Salmonella gallinarum, the causative agent of fowl typhoid, poses a persistent threat to poultry health and productivity, compounded by the growing problem of antibiotic resistance. Addressing the urgent need for effective alternatives, this study evaluated a multi-component complementary approach combining the phytocompound 4-hydroxycoumarin, silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), and Ajwain (Trachyspermum ammi) extract. In vitro assays, including antimicrobial susceptibility testing, cytotoxicity, and concentration optimization, confirmed the potent antibacterial activity and favorable safety profiles of the tested components. Molecular docking identified a putative interaction between 4-hydroxycoumarin and Chemokine (C-C motif) Ligand 5 (CCL5). Analysis of the archived molecular dynamics trajectory, after correction for periodic boundary conditions, revealed substantial protein conformational deviation and increasing ligand displacement toward the end of the trajectory, with a loss of close protein-ligand contact after approximately 40 ns. These findings support a predicted interaction but do not establish persistent ligand binding or a single predicted protein-ligand association mode. In the chicken infection model, the combination treatments were associated with descriptively reduced clinical severity and differences in endpoint mortality. These in vivo findings should be regarded as preliminary, descriptive, and exploratory proof-of-concept data, as mortality and clinical endpoint comparisons did not remain statistically significant after Holm correction. As 4-hydroxycoumarin was evaluated in vivo only as a component of the combination formulations, the observed effects belong strictly to the tested combinations, and their individual contributions cannot be determined independently. Gene expression analyses further revealed a downregulation of proinflammatory cytokines, providing exploratory evidence of immunomodulatory responses associated with the tested formulations. Together, these findings provide preliminary proof of concept for a multi-component approach against S. gallinarum infection.

title: Antifungal resistance in oral Candida: Phenotypic susceptibility, genomic surveillance, and novel postbiotic-based therapeutic strategies.
authors: Guhanraj R; Matharasi AP
abstract: Oral candidiasis is a common mucosal fungal infection, with Candida albicans remaining predominant alongside increasing recognition of non-albicans Candida species. Reduced antifungal susceptibility and resistance complicate laboratory diagnosis and treatment. This review summarizes current approaches to antifungal resistance characterization in oral Candida, including phenotypic susceptibility testing, molecular detection of resistance determinants, and whole-genome sequencing for strain characterization and genomic surveillance. Particular emphasis is placed on biofilm-associated tolerance, phenotypic adaptation, and mechanisms underlying reduced susceptibility. Emerging postbiotic-based strategies, including cell-free supernatants, bacteriocins, organic acids, biosurfactants, and extracellular vesicles, are also examined for their experimental activity against Candida growth, morphogenesis, adhesion, and biofilm formation. Integrating phenotypic and genomic approaches may strengthen resistance surveillance, while postbiotics warrant further standardized evaluation and clinical validation.

title: Sitagliptin attenuates urease-associated phenotypes and potentiates meropenem in multidrug-resistant Gram-negative clinical isolates: a preliminary repurposing study.
authors: Eladl A; Abbas HA; Abd El-Hamid MI; Elbaramawi SS; Noureldin NA; Nazeih SI
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Urease contributes to urinary tract pathogenesis and catheter encrustation, whereas metallo-β-lactamases contribute to carbapenem resistance.

OBJECTIVES: We investigated whether the dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor sitagliptin attenuates urease-associated phenotypes and potentiates meropenem against selected multidrug-resistant Gram-negative clinical isolates.

METHODS: Urease-associated activity was assessed in whole-cell suspensions and crude lysates of Proteus mirabilis. Alkalinization, crystal formation in artificial urine, and catheter-associated total biomass were also examined. Meropenem potentiation was evaluated by combined-disk and chequerboard assays, and meropenem-hydrolyzing activity was measured. Relative transcript abundance was assessed by quantitative reverse-transcription PCR, and docking was used to generate structural hypotheses. Vero-cell metabolic activity was evaluated by the MTT assay.

RESULTS: Sitagliptin (2000 µg/mL; one-eighth of its MIC) inhibited urease-associated assay signal by 53.2%-55.2% in whole-cell suspensions and crude lysates, reduced the urease-driven pH increase from 9.21 to 7.34 after 24 h, and reduced crystal-violet-stained catheter-associated biomass by 83.6%. It reduced the apparent meropenem hydrolysis signal in periplasmic extracts by 33%-55% and reduced meropenem MICs by 16- to 64-fold in combination assays, with FICI values of 0.1406-0.1875. In the Vero-cell assay, viability at 2000 µg/mL was 94.4%, and a 50% reduction in viability was not observed within the tested range. Sitagliptin exposure was associated with reduced relative transcript abundance of ureR, ureC, blaNDM, blaIMP, and blaVIM. Docking generated binding poses near catalytic metal centres.

CONCLUSIONS: In the tested preparations and isolate panel, sitagliptin attenuated urease-associated phenotypes, reduced apparent meropenem-hydrolyzing activity and potentiated meropenem, supporting its further investigation as a potential anti-virulence and antibiotic-adjuvant candidate.

title: Structural variant detection across sequencing technologies.
authors: Li G; Liu Y; Zhang A; Lin X; Hu Z; Liu B; Qian L; Wang Y
topics: Antimicrobial Resistance; Long-Read Microbiology; Bioinformatics Tools
abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are a major source of genomic diversity, yet their discovery remains challenging due to repetitive genomic contexts, alignment ambiguity and the trade-off between sequencing cost and read length. Here we introduce HitSV, which implements repetitiveness- and signature-density-aware breakpoint recognition coupled with precise haplotype-resolved local assembly, thereby enabling base-resolution SV reconstruction and genotyping in various sequencing technologies. On the HG002 benchmark, HitSV achieved 15-72% (long read), 10-36% (short read) and 12% (hybrid sequencing), respectively, higher genotype F1 scores than state-of-the-art SV callers. Applied to the 1KGP phase 4 cohort, HitSV expanded the SV callset by 31.5%, substantially reshaping allele-frequency landscapes. In a large Chinese long-read cohort, HitSV uncovered tandem-repeat-mobile-element composite arrays as a prevalent, multi-allelic class of complex SVs, highlighting composite repeat architectures as an important and previously underrecognized contributor to human structural variation.

title: FKS1/2-variant independent mechanisms underlying the emergence of resistance in echinocandin-refractory Candida auris infections.
authors: Gifford H; Pradhan A; Caswall B; Murphy SE; Leaves I; Edmondson MB; Chakraborty T; Wilson D; Taori SK; Gow NAR; Farrer RA; Brown AJP; Bicanic T
abstract: The emerging fungus Candida auris is a drug resistant global public health threat and WHO critical priority pathogen. Recommended first-line invasive candidiasis treatment is echinocandin monotherapy, but C. auris can develop on-treatment resistance via FKS1/2 gene mutations and additional, previously unexplained mechanisms. To better understand echinocandin failure in C. auris, we sequenced the genomes of echinocandin refractory FKS1/2 wild-type C. auris serial isolates from two critically unwell patients in London, UK. Population analysis profiling revealed echinocandin heteroresistance, and in vitro culture of clinical isolates at supra-MIC concentrations of anidulafungin (8 μg/ml) exhibited morphotypic heterogeneity. Small colony variants (SCVs) and large colony variants (LCVs) showed elevated MICs with polyploidy (to 4n and above) alongside adaptive changes in cell wall β-1,3-glucan content. LCVs contained significantly more mutations in calcineurin-related stress tolerance pathway gene CRZ1 compared to clinical parents and SCVs, associated with further increases in MIC. These findings indicate progressive step-wise accrual of adaptation to echinocandins, including genomic instability, alterations in stress tolerance pathways, and cell wall remodelling, paving the way for resistance emergence.

title: Mobile genetic elements drive a plasmid fusion and deletion lifecycle shaping evolution and antimicrobial resistance.
authors: Ipoutcha T; Wang Y; Rocha EPC; Penadés JR
abstract: Plasmids are key drivers of bacterial adaptation, yet the mechanisms that generate their diversity remain poorly understood. Here, we show that mobile genetic elements (MGEs) orchestrate a fusion-deletion life cycle that repeatedly remodels plasmids in Staphylococcus aureus. Large-scale genomic analyses reveal that multireplicon plasmids are widespread and strongly enriched in transposases. Using experimental assays, we demonstrate that rare MGE-mediated fusion events, via homologous recombination or transposition, combine distinct plasmids into single multireplicon elements, expanding gene content and transfer potential. Antibiotic pressure selectively enriches these fused plasmids, rescuing bacterial populations under stress, whereas opposing selective forces, including phage predation, favour deletion derivatives that preserve essential functions and phage transmissibility. This cyclical process generates dynamic plasmid repertoires with conserved backbones and diverse accessory modules. We propose that MGE-driven fusion-deletion cycles represent a general principle of plasmid evolution, explaining the rapid emergence and persistence of multidrug-resistant plasmids across bacterial pathogens.

title: The Piperacillin-Tazobactam MIC Behaves Like a Prognostic Marker, Not a Pharmacodynamic Exposure.
authors: Díez-Vidal A

title: Discordance without error: why antimicrobial susceptibility testing methods give different results and which result should we report?
authors: P S S; Sumri SHA; Joy R; Darping LP
abstract: Antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) methods may yield different results even when testing is technically correct and quality control is acceptable. This narrative review examines why disk diffusion, broth microdilution, gradient diffusion, commercial microdilution, and automated systems can produce discordant MICs, zone diameters, or interpretive categories. Method-dependent differences arise from broth-versus-agar environments, antimicrobial diffusion and stability, incubation conditions, inoculum effects, endpoint detection, concentration ranges, breakpoint proximity, heteroresistance, and delayed or inducible resistance expression. Importantly, method correctness does not guarantee method equivalence or suitability for every organism-antimicrobial combination. Current CLSI, EUCAST, and ISO principles are integrated with comparative evidence to determine which result should guide reporting when valid methods disagree. We propose a nine-step AST Discordance Resolution Framework that prioritizes pair-specific method suitability, quantitative result review, breakpoint proximity, known method limitations, and appropriate reference or confirmatory testing. Discordance should therefore prompt structured evidence-based resolution rather than automatic attribution to analytical laboratory error.

title: Genomic evidence of clonal and IncX3 plasmid-mediated dissemination of blaNDM-7 in the Klebsiella pneumoniae complex.
authors: Zhang Y; Ren G; Wu J; Xu J; Ji Y; Li G; Wang Z; Wang J; Jiao X; Sun L
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE), particularly those carrying New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM) variants, pose a major global health threat. Among these, NDM-7 has attracted increasing attention due to its enhanced carbapenemase activity and clinical relevance. This study investigated the prevalence, genomic characteristics and dissemination of blaNDM-7-positive Klebsiella pneumoniae complex isolates from clinical and environmental sources in Yangzhou, China.

METHODS: A total of 401 clinical isolates, 282 hospital surface swabs and 366 wastewater samples collected between 2018 and 2024 were screened for blaNDM. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing and whole-genome sequencing were performed to characterize resistance profiles, genomic features and phylogenetic relationships. Conjugation and serial-passage assays were used to assess plasmid transferability and stability, respectively.

RESULTS: Seven blaNDM-7-positive isolates were identified, including one clinical isolate, one hospital environmental isolate and five wastewater isolates. All exhibited multidrug resistance. The blaNDM-7 gene was located on highly conserved ∼46 kb IncX3 plasmids that exhibited high conjugation frequencies (10-5-10-4) and stability (96.0%-98.7% mean retention after approximately 600 generations). Phylogenetic analysis revealed close genomic relatedness among the six ST196 K. quasipneumoniae isolates recovered from different sources, with only 0-7 core-genome SNP differences. All six isolates were recovered within approximately 6 months, consistent with recent common ancestry and possible clonal dissemination across settings.

CONCLUSIONS: The close genomic relatedness of ST196 isolates from different sources supports possible clonal dissemination, while the high conservation, transferability and stability of IncX3 plasmids highlight their important role in the dissemination of blaNDM-7. These findings underscore the importance of continued genomic surveillance of blaNDM-7 and its associated mobile genetic elements across clinical and environmental settings.

title: Genomic Epidemiology and Antimicrobial Resistance Analyses of bla KPC-2-Producing Pseudomonas aeruginosa in Zhejiang, China.
authors: Bao S; Zhu L; Niu X; Tian J; Mao M; Shen W; Yu Q; Wang W
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC)-producing carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a global health burden due to its multidrug resistance. However, the resistance characteristics, molecular epidemiology, and dissemination mechanisms of bla KPC-2-producing carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa in China remain limited.

METHODS: A total of 23 bla KPC-2-producing carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa isolates were collected in a hospital in Jiaxing, Zhejiang, from February 2021 to January 2025. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing and whole-genome sequencing were performed. Multilocus sequence typing, antimicrobial resistance genes, and virulence factors were identified. Phylogenetic analyses were performed, and genetic context analyses were conducted.

RESULTS: Six sequence types (STs) were identified among 23 isolates, with ST463 accounting for 56.5%. All isolates exhibited multidrug-resistant phenotypes and were identified as carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa. 17.4% of isolates showed resistance to ceftazidime/avibactam (CZA). All ST463 isolates co-harbored exoS and exoU. The core-genome MLST analysis identified two clusters within ST463 isolates, and the core-genome single-nucleotide polymorphism analysis revealed close genomic relatedness among ST4424 and ST4526 isolates. The bla KPC-2 genetic context was mainly associated with an ISKpn27-bla KPC-ISKpn6-like structure and IncU-related sequences.

CONCLUSION: ST463 was identified as the predominance lineage among bla KPC-2-producing carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa in this study, and multidrug resistance genes and multiple virulence factor genes in the ST463 were demonstrated. Genomic analyses identified closely related isolates consistent with potential nosocomial transmission in the hospital. These findings highlighted the importance of continuous genomic surveillance, susceptibility monitoring, and strengthened infection control strategies for limiting the persistence and potential nosocomial spread of high-risk bla KPC-2-producing carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa.

title: Targeted next-generation sequencing: a promising approach for pathogen and antimicrobial resistance gene detection in urinary tract infections.
authors: Gao W; Han W; Chen J; Gao Z; Gao J; Zhen R; Yuan Y; Gu Y; Huang C; Liu C; Wang G; Zhang X; Zhao Z; Xiong G; Li X; Zhu P; Liu J; Hu C; Gong Y; Zhang Z
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are common and frequently recurrent. As traditional diagnostic methods fail to meet clinical needs, this study aimed to construct and evaluate the performance of targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) for detecting pathogens and antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) in urine specimens.

METHODS: A total of 446 urine samples from patients with suspected UTIs were tested by tNGS, routine culture, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), with discordant results resolved by metagenomic NGS (mNGS) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS). The performance of tNGS was evaluated against culture and a composite reference standard (CRS) for pathogen detection, and against AST and WGS for resistance prediction.

RESULTS: tNGS achieved limit of detections of 500-1,000 CFU/mL, with high precision. Compared to culture, tNGS achieved a higher positive rate (62.78%), along with an overall sensitivity of 90.05% and specificity of 56.28%, whereas against the CRS the sensitivity and specificity reached 99.54% and 97.49%, respectively. For the seven common UTI bacteria, both metrics exceeded 90% regardless of the reference standard. Additionally, tNGS outperformed culture in detecting hard-to-culture microbes and polymicrobial infections. Among 132 samples with available AST results, ARG-based prediction showed strong concordance with resistance phenotypes for carbapenems (100.00%) and third generation cephalosporins + β-lactamase inhibitors (91.67%). Factors including sex and urine leukocyte count > 10 cells/μL were found associated with positive tNGS results.

CONCLUSION: tNGS enables rapid, sensitive and comprehensive detection of UTI pathogens and ARGs, covering hard-to-culture pathogens and mixed infections, thereby showing promise in improving diagnosis. However, it complements rather than replaces phenotypic AST, particularly for penicillin-class antibiotics.

title: Antifungal susceptibility and genomic profile associated with biosynthetic gene clusters of bovine mastitis-derived Aspergillus fumigatus DAH1043FM.
authors: Prajapati A; Parmar P; Chavan M; Chandra V; Shekh S; Patel A; Sabara P; Kanani A; Bagatharia S; Jha CK
abstract: The most frequently isolated fungus from mycotic mastitis in cattle is Aspergillus fumigatus, which can cause infection by germinating on the animal's surface to form hyphae that penetrate epithelial and endothelial barriers and initiate mastitis. In this study, the fungal strain DAH1043FM was isolated from the milk of a cow with mastitis and identified as Aspergillus fumigatus by internal transcribed spacer (ITS) region sequencing. Species identity was further confirmed by whole-genome Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI) analysis. A. fumigatus DAH1043FM showed minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values of 0.5 μg/mL for amphotericin B and itraconazole, 0.12 μg/mL for posaconazole and voriconazole, 128 μg/mL for fluconazole, and >8 μg/mL for caspofungin, micafungin, and anidulafungin. Comparative Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) with two reference genomes of A. fumigatus, Af293 and A1163, was used to identify genetic variants, such as single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and other mutations, in genes associated with antifungal resistance, including those involved in drug efflux, ergosterol biosynthesis, echinocandin target pathways, and other resistance-related processes. Furthermore, genome mining identified biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) showing substantial similarity to characterized pathways associated with fumiquinazoline (100%), gliotoxin (84%), fumagillin (80%), and trypacidin (71%). These results demonstrate that strain DAH1043FM carries predicted genetic variants in target pathways while exhibiting wild-type susceptibility to azoles alongside off-scale endpoints for echinocandins. Genome analysis of strain DAH1043FM identified predicted secondary metabolite BGCs, highlighting the value of genome-level surveillance for fungal isolates recovered from bovine milk.

title: Compound Z247611722 Exhibits Antifungal Activity by Inhibiting Serine Palmitoyltransferase.
authors: Nysten J; Van Eynde W; Lee Y; Vanhoffelen E; Desiderati G; Van Win T; Vande Velde G; Voet A; Robbins N; Cowen LE; Van Dijck P
abstract: The global rise in fungal infections, driven by expanding at-risk populations and growing antifungal resistance, highlights the need for new therapies. However, the current antifungal arsenal remains limited and emerging resistance reduces treatment efficacy. Through high-throughput screening of 20,000 drug-like compounds, we identified Z56812898, a benzamide linked to a bicyclic pyrimidine-pyran trione with novel antifungal activity. Guided by this hit, we discovered a structural analog with improved antifungal potency, Z247611722. This fungicidal compound has novel antifungal activity against multiple Candida species and fluconazole-resistant isolates. Chemogenomic, metabolomic, and phenotypic analyses revealed that Z247611722 disrupts sphingolipid biosynthesis by targeting serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT). The mode of action was confirmed by experimental evolution, yielding a resistant strain with a non-synonymous mutation in the SPT-encoding gene, LCB2. Structural modelling localized this alanine-to-proline substitution adjacent to the catalytic cavity, where it could alter the dynamics and conformation of the binding pocket and impair compound accommodation. Importantly, Z247611722 demonstrates in vivo efficacy in an invertebrate model of C. albicans infection. These findings validate SPT as a promising target and introduce a structurally distinct sphingolipid biosynthesis inhibitor with therapeutic potential.

title: Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic evaluation of multidose oritavancin for prolonged durations of therapy.
authors: Volk CF; Blumenthal M; Thomas N; Kufel WD; Rose WE; Lim SY
abstract: Managing multidrug-resistant gram-positive infections is challenging, especially when prolonged therapy is needed for conditions like bacteremia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, or other deep-seated infections. Oritavancin, a long-acting lipoglycopeptide, is increasingly used in these scenarios and offers an alternative to central catheter placement. However, despite its growing use for extended treatment, optimal dosing strategies and pharmacokinetic targets remain unclear. An in silico pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic simulation was performed to assess the predicted oritavancin concentration resulting from weekly and every 2-week dosing regimens. The simulations utilized a previously published model, which utilized pharmacokinetic sampling data from two single-dose, phase 3 clinical trials. A 100% free time above the MIC was utilized as the pharmacodynamic target. The Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute breakpoint (0.12 µg/mL) and MIC90 (0.06 µg/mL) values for both Staphylococcus aureus and Enterococcus faecalis were utilized as benchmarks. Eighty-five percent protein binding was assumed. A six-dose regimen of 1,200 mg weekly is expected to maintain free plasma concentrations above the breakpoint for a median of 10.4 weeks (lower 5th percentile 9.6) and above the MIC90 for about 1.5 weeks longer, exceeding what is usually required for acute treatment of most infections. Alternatively, using a three-dose regimen of 1,200 mg every 2 weeks is expected to maintain free plasma concentrations above the breakpoint for a median of 8.4 weeks (lower 5th percentile 7.9), with trough values remaining therapeutic between doses. Every 2-week dosing strategies are expected to maintain therapeutic concentrations between doses. This strategy may be employed to reduce the cost of treatment and improve patient convenience.

title: Daptomycin for enterococcal bloodstream infections and endocarditis: reconciling clinical evidence, susceptibility testing, and regulatory frameworks.
authors: Díez-Vidal A; Vizcarra P; Oñoro-López CM; Marcelo-Calvo C; de Gea Grela A; Díaz-Pollán B; García-Rodríguez J; Cacho J; Arribas JR
abstract: Despite the absence of US Food and Drug Administration or European Medicines Agency approval, randomised trials, and harmonised susceptibility guidance, daptomycin has become indispensable for the treatment of serious enterococcal bloodstream infections and endocarditis. The Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute assigns Enterococcus faecium a susceptible dose-dependent category (≤4 mg/L, 8-12 mg/kg per day) and Enterococcus faecalis a susceptible breakpoint (≤2 mg/L, 6 mg/kg per day), whereas the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing sets no clinical breakpoint, citing insufficient evidence. We argue that this misalignment between evidence and regulation is itself a potential source of patient harm, through persistent underdosing and inconsistent interpretive guidance. Observational data link 10-12 mg/kg per day with lower mortality in patients infected with vancomycin-resistant E faecium. Even so, appropriate dosing frequently does not attain the pharmacodynamic target, because target attainment depends less on the administered dose than on the isolate's minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), which current methods cannot reliably determine. Any-grade creatine phosphokinase elevation rises modestly with dose in the largest registry but is inconsistent elsewhere, with a clearer signal of marked elevation at the highest doses. We propose a pragmatic framework (≥8 mg/kg per day for E faecium, 10-12 mg/kg per day in vancomycin-resistant disease, MIC-informed dose selection, β-lactam combination in endocarditis, and weekly creatine phosphokinase monitoring) and call for therapeutic drug monitoring, harmonised breakpoints, prospective studies, and molecular resistance detection.

title: Performance evaluation of antimicrobial susceptibility testing devices across CLSI, EUCAST, ISO, FDA, and EMA frameworks: implications for breakpoint application.
authors: Shindikar A; Mahesh R; Periasamy H; Vaidya S
abstract: Broth microdilution (BMD) remains the reference standard for determining minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) in antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST). However, most routine laboratories rely on surrogate methods, including disk diffusion and commercial MIC-generating systems, whose results must correlate with those of reference BMD prior to clinical use. Evaluation criteria differ across standards development organizations (SDOs) and regulatory authorities, potentially affecting clinical interpretation, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This mini-review compares evaluation frameworks from major SDOs-the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI), the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST), and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO)-and regulatory frameworks, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR). Key performance metrics, including essential agreement, categorical agreement, error rates, reproducibility, and bias, were analyzed, alongside differences in breakpoint setting and device approval pathways. Implications for clinical microbiology and antimicrobial stewardship were considered, with explicit emphasis on challenges faced in LMIC settings. Substantial heterogeneity exists across frameworks. CLSI and FDA emphasize breakpoint-dependent categorical agreement and error rates, whereas ISO prioritizes analytical measures such as essential agreement and bias without categorical errors. EUCAST broadly aligns with ISO analytically while separately maintaining responsibility for breakpoint setting. These differences can yield discordant device assessments, especially after breakpoint revisions. Surrogate MICs often correlate with BMD near breakpoints but may show systematic bias across MIC ranges, not fully captured by essential agreement alone, with important implications for LMIC laboratories. Divergent frameworks influence susceptibility interpretation, resistance surveillance, and antimicrobial stewardship, particularly in LMICs. Greater harmonization and awareness of methodological limitations are essential to ensure reliable AST reporting and support global antimicrobial resistance efforts across LMIC healthcare systems.

title: First report of proven Fusarium brachygibbosum sinusitis in a paediatric patient with acute myeloblastic leukaemia.
authors: Maldonado-Barrueco A; Del Castillo YM; Baquero-Artigao F; Grasa C; Del Valle de León N; Martínez-Romera I; de Asua IF; Alastruey-Izquierdo A; Alcázar-Fuoli L; Quiles-Melero I; García-Rodríguez J
journal: Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis
abstract:
PURPOSE: Fusarium brachygibbosum is an environmental mould belonging to the Fusarium sambucinum species complex (FSAMSC) and is only exceptionally reported as a human pathogen. Invasive fusariosis is a recognized complication in patients with hematological malignancies; however, proven infection caused by F. brachygibbosum has not previously been described. We report the first case of proven breakthrough sinusitis in a pediatric female with refractory acute myeloblastic leukaemia (AML) receiving posaconazole prophylaxis.

METHODS: We describe the clinical presentation, microbiological diagnosis, antifungal susceptibility profile, treatment, and outcome of a 13-year-old neutropenic female with refractory AML who developed invasive fungal sinusitis. Species identification was established by Sanger sequencing of the elongation factor 1-alpha, and antifungal susceptibility testing was performed according to the EUCAST reference method.

RESULTS: Computed tomography revealed extensive paranasal sinus involvement, and direct microscopy of sinus tissue demonstrated hyaline septate hyphae. Culture yielded a mould initially misidentified by MALDI-TOF MS as F. chlamydosporium. Molecular sequencing confirmed F. brachygibbosum. The isolate exhibited elevated Minimal inhibitory concentrations (MICs) to amphotericin B, azoles, echinocandins, and olorofim, while fosmanogepix showed a lower in vitro MIC. Extensive surgical debridement combined with liposomal amphotericin B, voriconazole, and subsequently olorofim was performed. Despite local control of the sinonasal infection and no microbiological or histopathological evidence of dissemination, the patient died 23 days after diagnosis. The death occurred in the context of progressive refractory AML, invasive fungal disease, pulmonary abnormalities, and subsequent neutropenic complications.

CONCLUSION: This report represents the first proven pediatric case of invasive sinusitis caused by F. brachygibbosum (FSAMSC) isolate with higher MICs to classical antifungals. The case highlights the diagnostic limitations of MALDI-TOF MS for rare Fusarium species, the value of molecular identification and antifungal susceptibility testing, and the emergence of environmental moulds breakthrough fungal infections. It also underscores the urgent need for effective novel antifungal agents against resistant Fusarium species.

title: Decoding the genomic repertoire of fosfomycin resistance genes in staphylococci.
authors: Chen Y; Zhu F; Ye M; Hong Y; Wang P; Wang H; Wang Z; Du X; Sun L; Yu Y; Chen Y
abstract: Fosfomycin is regaining clinical relevance for multidrug-resistant staphylococcal infections, yet the diversity, evolutionary origin and nomenclature of staphylococcal fosfomycin resistance genes remain inconsistently defined. We surveyed 17,024 publicly available genomes representing 14 clinically common Staphylococcus species to curate a catalogue of fosfomycin-modifying fos homologues. By integrating amino-acid identity, phylogenetic topology, genomic context and population-level distribution, we established a reproducible classification framework that resolved species- or lineage-associated intrinsic genes, including fosSA, fosSE, fosSC, fosSCp and fosSL, from acquired determinants, including fosB, fosD, fosY and ten prophage-associated families designated fosSΦA-J. Intrinsic genes showed conserved local contexts, whereas prophage-borne determinants occupied diverse insertion sites, supporting distinct evolutionary trajectories. Functional assays showed variable effects on fosfomycin susceptibility. Deleting fosSA in MRSA reduced the fosfomycin MIC 16-fold, and complementation restored resistance. This study provides a unified nomenclature and evolutionary framework for staphylococcal fos genes and highlights the need to monitor both lineage-associated and mobile fos determinants.

title: Comparison of antimicrobial susceptibility testing methods for aztreonam-avibactam against NDM-producing Enterobacterales clinical isolates.
authors: Rivas L; Díaz L; Quiroz V; Martinez JRW; Solar C; Khan A; Soto K; Rojas Soto P; Acuña M-P; Rioseco ML; Mühlhauser M; Bergman Y; García P; Munita JM; Tamma PD
abstract: Aztreonam-avibactam (ATM-AVI) is a promising therapeutic for New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales (NDM-E) infections. We evaluated the performance of disk diffusion and gradient diffusion methods compared with reference broth microdilution (BMD) for ATM-AVI susceptibility testing. A total of 245 non-duplicate NDM-E isolates were included, collected from unique patients at hospitals in Chile and the United States between 2022 and 2024. Nine ATM-AVI non-susceptible isolates from a separate collection were added to enrich for resistant isolates, yielding a total of 254 isolates. Reference BMD was performed according to Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) criteria. ATM-AVI disk diffusion and two gradient diffusion methods (ETEST and MIC Test Strip) were evaluated against BMD using categorical agreement, essential agreement, and CLSI-defined error rates. All 245 NDM-E isolates were susceptible to ATM-AVI (MIC ≤4/4 µg/mL), with MIC₅₀/₉₀ values of 0.25/4 and 1/4 µg/mL, respectively. The collection consisted of Klebsiella pneumoniae (71%), Enterobacter cloacae complex (21%), and Escherichia coli (8%). Predominant NDM alleles included blaNDM-1 and blaNDM-7. Disk diffusion demonstrated 98% categorical agreement (250/254), with four minor errors. Both gradient diffusion methods achieved 99% categorical agreement (252/254), with no very major or major errors and two minor errors. Essential agreement was 67% for ETEST and 85% for MIC Test Strip; both methods tended to underestimate ATM-AVI MICs relative to BMD. ATM-AVI demonstrated robust in vitro activity against a contemporary NDM-E cohort. Disk and gradient diffusion methods are practical alternatives to BMD for clinical laboratories.

title: Toward routine implementation of phage testing: an inter-laboratory comparison of a disk-based susceptibility testing (Disk-PST).
authors: Ekat K; Scharnagl L; Hahn A; Deinhardt-Emmer S; Trimborn A; Landtag J; Wietzke M; Elias J; Lestin-Bernstein F; Splettstoesser W; Ramming I; Knobloch JK; Färber J; Szabados F; Podbielski A; Warnke P; Skusa R
abstract: In the context of an emerging post-antibiotic era, phage therapy is gaining increasing attention. Standardized approaches for phage susceptibility testing (PST) are crucial to enable objective and effective phage selection for personalized treatment, yet no standardized reference method currently exists. To overcome this impediment, a standardized disk-based PST protocol was validated in-house (intra-laboratory comparison) involving 28 participants, followed by an inter-laboratory comparison across 12 laboratories in Germany with 39 participants. Preselection testing revealed high concordance between Disk-PST and Spot test, supporting the selection of strains with consistent phage susceptibility profiles for the interlaboratory comparison. An Escherichia coli phage, a Staphylococcus epidermidis phage, and a negative control (SM buffer) were tested on four bacterial strains (two E. coli and two S. epidermidis strains). Testing was blinded and included two technical and two biological replicates per condition. The plaque assay was performed at the coordinating laboratory (University Medical Center Rostock) and served as the reference standard. The in-house validation showed high reliability and strong agreement with the plaque assay, requiring only minor methodological adjustments prior to the inter-laboratory trial. The inter-laboratory comparison confirmed the robustness of the method, showing almost perfect agreement with the plaque assay across all participating laboratories. In the rare event of false-positive or inconclusive results, phage cross-contamination, misinterpretation of microcolonies within lysis zones, and limited information on negative controls due to the blinded test setting were causative. In accordance with its high inter-laboratory reliability, the PST-disk method seems to be highly suitable for easy implementation in routine laboratory settings. Further investigations are necessary to correlate phage test results with clinical therapy outcomes-an issue that should be addressed in future clinical trials.IMPORTANCEThe rapid global spread of multidrug-resistant bacteria has intensified the need for effective alternative therapeutic strategies, including bacteriophage therapy. Because phage activity is highly strain-specific, accurate and standardized phage susceptibility testing (PST) is essential for safe and effective clinical implementation, yet standardized protocols are currently lacking. In this nationwide, blinded inter-laboratory study, we evaluated a routine-diagnostic-adapted single-disk PST method and demonstrated its excellent agreement with the gold-standard double agar layer plaque assay. Importantly, this approach represents a significant improvement over existing PST methods by providing a standardized, reproducible, and easy-to-implement assay with high potential for widespread application in clinical routine microbiology laboratories.

title: Deep learning recognises antibiotic modes of action from brightfield images.
authors: Krentzel D; Kho K; Petit J; Mahtal N; Delerue T; Huber ME; Zettor A; Chiaravalli J; Shorte SL; Brönstrup M; Wehenkel AM; Boneca IG; Zimmer C
abstract: The antimicrobial resistance crisis urgently calls for antibiotics with novel modes of action (MoAs). While growth inhibition assays can identify antibiotic molecules, they miss promising compounds below inhibitory concentrations and cannot reveal their MoA. Imaging-based profiling of drug-treated bacteria can inform on MoA, but current approaches generally require fluorescent labelling and/or inhibitory concentrations and it remains unclear whether compounds with novel MoAs can be robustly detected. Here, we demonstrate a deep learning approach to recognise antibiotic MoAs from unlabelled images. We train a convolutional neural network to predict treatment conditions from brightfield images of Escherichia coli exposed to antibiotics covering eight MoAs. Our approach can detect drug exposure at subinhibitory concentrations and allows near-perfect MoA recognition, even when trained on only eight images per treatment condition. Previously unseen compounds are assigned to their correct MoA with good accuracy if the MoA is represented in the training data, and our method can robustly detect MoA novelty in five out of six considered MoAs, enabling microscopy-based identification of new antibiotic classes. We also achieve near-perfect MoA recognition in Klebsiella pneumoniae, suggesting applicability to other species. Our approach complements growth inhibition assays and is poised to improve the search for innovative antibiotic compounds.

title: Multimodal substrate recruitment enables CTLHMKLN1 E3 ligase to target acetylated N-, C-, and internal degrons.
authors: Sepic S; Gottemukkala KV; Du J; Maiwald SA; Chrustowicz J; Papadopoulou EC; Stier LJ; von Gronau S; Schulman BA
abstract: The GID/CTLH family of E3 ubiquitin ligases employs several substrate receptor subunits that recruit distinct degrons, but the substrate recognition mechanisms of the CTLHMKLN1 assembly have largely remained elusive. Here, we reconstitute CTLHMKLN1-dependent ubiquitylation of three biochemically distinct substrates - MKLN1 itself, ZMYND19, and FAM72A-recruited UNG2, and determine cryo-EM structures of each substrate bound to MKLN1. The structures reveal how MKLN1's discoidin and Kelch β-propeller domains engage substrates through multivalent contacts. MKLN1 recruits itself through discoidin-Kelch interactions between MKLN1 dimers, forming an assembly that competes with other substrates. ZMYND19 and FAM72A each bind to MKLN1 through loops engaging the discoidin trench domain while their C-terminal Arg residues engage the MKLN1 Kelch central channel, identifying MKLN1 as an Arg/C-degron receptor. The acetylated N-terminus of UNG2 is positioned within a Y-shaped tunnel of FAM72A, defining an adaptor-mediated Ac/N-degron recognition mechanism. Thus, our data reveal how combinatorial deployment of MKLN1 discoidin and Kelch domains enable a single receptor subunit to recognize a diverse substrate repertoire, adding to a complex picture of degron recognition across the GID/CTLH family.

title: Long-term spatiotemporal dynamics of β-lactamase resistome in the Han River, South Korea.
authors: Lee DH; Kim YS; Kim DW; Kim DS; Cha CJ
abstract: The global dissemination of antimicrobial resistance, particularly resistance to widely prescribed β-lactam antibiotics, is a critical public health threat worldwide. Aquatic ecosystems act as key reservoirs where antibiotic resistance genes accumulate and are transmitted between environmental bacteria and human pathogens within a One Health framework. To move beyond short-term observations and better understand these cross-sectoral dynamics, we conducted 5-year longitudinal surveillance using shotgun metagenomics across different seasons along the Han River, South Korea. Our analysis revealed a diverse repertoire of β-lactamases, predominantly belonging to Ambler classes A and D, which also accounted for most mobile β-lactamase genes and were enriched in densely populated downstream regions. Furthermore, β-lactamase genes exhibited clear seasonal fluctuations, with a pronounced winter surge in total and mobile β-lactamase gene abundances. We also identified a substantial fraction of novel variants, whose abundance and composition varied across spatial and seasonal gradients. Network analysis revealed that the genera Pseudomonas and Klebsiella acted as primary hosts, with their mobile β-lactamase genes highly connected to multiple taxa, suggesting important roles in β-lactamase gene transmission. These findings suggest that preemptive management of aquatic β-lactamase genes is a fundamental strategy for mitigating future resistance crises within a One Health framework and provide critical evidence for identifying transmission pathways and tracking resistance evolution between natural and clinical environments.

title: High-fiber diet altered gut microbiota, improved glycemic control, and reduced body weight in newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes and obesity.
authors: Li Y; Liu Y; Chen Y; Xiang B; Fu H; Pan H; Xu T; Li Z; Zhang Y; Yuan H; Zhang C
abstract: Type 2 diabetes and obesity commonly coexist, making glycemia and body weight both central treatment goals. Few trials have directly compared a high-fiber dietary intervention with metformin. The factors associated with individual responses to high-fiber diet also remain unclear. In this single-center, open-label, head-to-head clinical trial, 48 adults with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity were randomized to a high-fiber dietary intervention without glucose-lowering medication (n = 36) or metformin (n = 12) monotherapy for 84 days; 46 completed the trial. Clinical outcomes and 184 fecal samples were assessed longitudinally using shotgun metagenomic and metabolite profiling. At Day 84, the high-fiber group had greater reductions in glycated hemoglobin and body mass index and lower glycemic variability than the metformin group. The diet altered gut microbiota by Day 28, enriching genomes from Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus and depleting genomes from Bilophila wadsworthia, but metformin produced little detectable microbiota change. These changes included increased acetate-production functions and decreased hydrogen sulfide-production functions; fecal hydrogen sulfide was lower at Days 28 and 56, although short-chain fatty acid concentrations did not differ between groups at matched time points. Within the high-fiber group, participants with increased fecal acetate (25 of 34) had larger glycated hemoglobin reductions at Days 28 and 56, and baseline microbial features differed between acetate-response subgroups. These findings support high-fiber diet as a non-pharmacologic strategy for diabesity, with baseline microbial features as candidate markers of response. Clinical trial registration: ChiCTR-INR-17011752.

title: Structural and functional characterization of the gut microbiota in women with early pregnancy loss in Northwest China.
authors: Yao H; Chen J; Liu C; Huang J; Liu L; Wang Q; Wang F
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early pregnancy loss (EPL) is a common adverse pregnancy outcome with a complex and incompletely understood etiology. Moreover, metagenomic studies of the gut microbiota in women with EPL in Northwest China remain limited.

OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to characterize differences in gut microbial composition and predicted functional potential between women with EPL (EPL group) and normal controls (NCs) using shotgun metagenomic sequencing.

METHODS: We collected fecal samples from 216 women in Northwest China (EPL group, n = 72; NCs, n = 144). Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed to analyze gut microbiota composition and assess the functional potential of the microbiota.

RESULTS: Our study revealed significant differences in the composition of the gut microbiota between the EPL group and NCs, as assessed by alpha and beta diversity analyses (p < 0.001). Bacteroides was significantly more abundant in the EPL group, whereas Coprococcus, Bifidobacterium, and Roseburia were significantly more abundant in NCs. Compared to NCs, the EPL group had higher relative abundances of species such as Bacteroides stercoris, Bacteroides plebeius, and Bacteroides uniformis, but lower relative abundances of Bifidobacterium adolescentis, Megamonas funiformis, and Fusicatenibacter saccharivorans. Partial correlation analysis showed that Bacteroidetes was positively correlated with EPL at the phylum level. At the genus level, Odoribacter, Parabacteroides, and Haemophilus were positively correlated with EPL, whereas Corynebacterium, Lactobacillus, and Roseburia were negatively correlated with EPL. Metabolic pathway analysis revealed that pathways such as L-rhamnose degradation I, L-arginine biosynthesis III and 2-oxobutanoate degradation I exhibited significant positive correlations with EPL. In contrast, pathways including purine nucleobases degradation I (anaerobic) and chitin derivatives degradation showed significant negative correlations with EPL.

CONCLUSION: The results of our study revealed significant differences in gut microbiota composition and metabolic pathways between the EPL group and NCs, indicating that gut microbiome alterations are associated with EPL.

title: DNAharvester: A Nextflow Pipeline for Analysing Highly Degraded DNA from Ancient and Historical Specimens.
authors: Sharif B; Kutschera VE; Oskolkov N; Guinet B; Lord E; Chacón-Duque JC; Oppenheimer J; van der Valk T; Del-Molino DD; Heintzman PD; Dalén L
abstract:
MOTIVATION: Ancient DNA (aDNA) research has advanced rapidly with the development of high-throughput sequencing, enabling genome-wide analyses of large collections of prehistoric specimens. However, analysing palaeontological and archaeological material with highly degraded DNA constitutes a major bioinformatic challenge. DNA from such samples is characterized by short fragment lengths, low endogenous content, post-mortem damage, and cross-species contamination, which can increase spurious mapping and reference bias, affecting downstream population genetic inferences.

RESULTS: We present DNAharvester, a modular and reproducible pipeline designed specifically for processing highly degraded DNA from ancient and historical specimens. DNAharvester integrates metagenomic filtering, competitive mapping, adaptive aligner selection (incorporating BWA-aln, BWA-mem, and Bowtie2), and systematic evaluation of reference bias and spurious mapping. By incorporating flexible mapping and filtering strategies, the pipeline can be adapted to varying sample preservation, focusing on maximizing authentic data recovery. DNAharvester features subworkflows for iterative assembly of mitogenomes, identification of genomic repeats and CpG sites, taxonomic classification, microbial/pathogen screening, genetic sex determination, and variant calling. To accommodate varying sequencing depths, the pipeline supports diploid variant calling, genotype likelihood estimation, and pseudo-haploid random allele calling. We validated the pipeline using simulated and empirical datasets, demonstrating its ability to systematically mitigate complex background contamination while preserving authentic genomic signals. By streamlining complex bioinformatic tasks through simple configuration files, DNAharvester establishes a standardized approach for analysing aDNA datasets and makes genomic analyses of ancient remains accessible to the broader research community.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Implemented in Nextflow, DNAharvester provides a highly scalable, containerized framework that enhances reproducibility, portability, and robustness in aDNA analyses. DNAharvester is open source under the GNU General Public License v3.0 and freely available at https://github.com/NBISweden/DNAharvester.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online and Zenodo repository: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22725211.

title: Effect of dietary chickpea structures on the small intestine metabolome and microbiome: a randomised crossover trial.
authors: Fernandes N; Cai M; Warren FJ; Duncan A; Harris H; Serrano Contreras JI; Sidorczuk K; Bernal A; Castillo A; Petropoulou K; Blunt D; Perez-Moral N; Garcia-Perez I; Edwards C; Hildebrand F; Holmes E; Wist J; Frost G
abstract: The human gastrointestinal tract (GIT) is central to human physiology, yet our understanding of the metabolite, microbial, and hormonal spatiotemporal dynamics in humans is limited. How these environments respond to complex food structures and homeostatic mechanisms they generate is unknown in humans. In this randomised study, ten participants consumed chickpea-based meals with intact versus broken cellular structures, with sampling of oral, gastric, duodenal and ileal fluids. The primary outcome was the postprandial enteroendocrine hormone responses (GIP, GLP-1 and PYY); secondary outcomes were GIT metabolite profiles (1H NMR) and ileal microbiota (shotgun metagenomics). We observed that food structure markedly altered the spatiotemporal trajectories of metabolites and dominant microbe, driving distinct enteroendocrine hormone responses. Broken-cell meals produced early GIT glucose and maltose peaks associated with rapid GIP responses, whereas intact-cell meals elevated duodenal amino acids and ileal sugars, amino acids and formate, enhancing GLP-1 and PYY responses. Microbial profiles exhibited rapid spatial reorganisation, with evidence that oral bacterial strains transmitted to the ileum, where their abundance was associated with local metabolites and PYY responses. These findings identify food structure as a determinant of postprandial gastrointestinal metabolism and enteroendocrine responses and suggest an underappreciated route for oral bacteria to reach the ileum via the food bolus and impact metabolism. ISRCTN registration: ISRCTN18097249.

title: PanRes: A database of latent and acquired antimicrobial resistance allowing 3D-based protein homology search.
authors: Vojtková M; Baltušis M; Martiny HM; Baral A; Pyrounakis N; Beleon A; Freitag R; Pico-Tomàs A; Kaas RS; Petersen TN; Munk P
abstract:
MOTIVATION: Antimicrobial resistance databases are central to genomic surveillance, but resistance determinants remain distributed across resources with different scopes, structures, and annotations.

RESULTS: We developed PanRes, a curated resistance database of 11 717 genes integrating acquired and latent determinants of antibiotic, biocide, and metal resistance within a unified ontology. We predicted representative protein structures and clustered them by structural similarity, grouping proteins into 505 high-confidence structurally conserved clusters coherent despite sequence divergence. Their structure-guided alignments were used to build Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) for remote homology search. In seven wastewater metagenomes from five European cities, PanRes 3D-based HMMs expanded detection beyond what was possible with BLAST, with 35.3% of retained hits identified only by the HMMs and generally showing greater divergence from known proteins. For beta-lactamases, several proteins retained beta-lactamase-like folds and catalytic geometry despite weak sequence similarity.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: PanRes is available through an interactive web platform (https://panres.rambio.dk/), a structure-informed resource for exploring the whole resistome. The database, HMM profiles, and ontology are available at Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.22876216).

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Targeted long-read eukaryotic profiling of human stool by broad-range 18S-28S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing on Oxford Nanopore Technologies: a proof-of-concept study.
authors: Kalendar R; Daniyarov A; Kairov U; Kozhakhmetov S; Yerezhepov D; Yermekbayeva B; Sarbassov D; Kushugulova A
abstract: The gut eukaryome, comprising the protists and fungi that fall within the strict definition of the microbiota together with the macroscopic helminths and arthropods that lie outside it, is under-detected by clinical microscopy and by short-read 16S/18S sequencing, yet is increasingly implicated in inflammatory and autoimmune disorders, including psoriasis. Existing 18S V4/V9 primers either lack cross-kingdom universality or fail to discriminate closely related species. We designed and evaluated broad-range PCR primers anchored in conserved blocks of nuclear 18S and 28S ribosomal genes, flanking a 1.0-3.5 kb cassette spanning the 3'-end of 18S, ITS1, 5.8S, ITS2, and the 5'-end of 28S. Stool samples from 91 plaque-psoriasis patients and 92 matched controls were collected; a subset of 32 samples was profiled by Oxford Nanopore amplicon sequencing using the EPI2ME wf-metagenomics pipeline (Kraken + Bracken) against the NCBI core_nt database. The gut eukaryome was dominated by Ascomycota and Protista, with 51 species-level entries assigned to Candida (37 named binomials), 27 entries assigned to Blastocystis (12 subtype-labelled entries), 20 entries assigned to Malassezia (15 named species), and 37 entries assigned to Cladosporium recovered from a single PCR tube. Blastocystis hominis was detected in 37.5% of subjects (≥50-read threshold; mean 7.5% in carriers), with concurrent detection of 12 subtype-labelled entries (ST1-ST4, ST7, ST10-ST15, ST24) and 11 named isolate entries. Psoriasis-relevant Candida species, such as C. albicans (34.4%), C. tropicalis (34.4%), C. parapsilosis (31.2%), and Malassezia restricta (9.4%; up to 12.1%) were co-detected. Long-read sequencing of a broad-range 18S -28S rRNA gene cassette provides a single-tube workflow for the simultaneous recovery of fungal, protistan, and plant-derived eukaryotic sequences from human stool.

title: Identification and characteristics of multiple viruses in snow leopard fecal samples using viral metagenomics.
authors: Xue Y; Cai S; Ji L; Ji L; Shen Q; Wang X; Wu P; Liu Y; Wang Y; Zhang W; Yang S
abstract: Metagenomic studies on the fecal virome of snow leopards, rare apex predators on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP), remain limited. In this study, we utilized metagenomic sequencing to characterize the fecal viral community in captive QTP snow leopards. We assembled 22 complete viral genomes across the families Anelloviridae, Circoviridae, Parvoviridae, Picornaviridae, Genomoviridae, and Smacoviridae. Phylogenetic analyses indicated substantial sequence novelty. We identified 9 anellovirus genomes in the genera Tettorquevirus and Etatorquevirus, 3 candidate novel parvoviruses in Bocaparvovirus, Chaphamaparvovirus, and Dependoparvovirus, 3 circovirus genomes representing 2 candidate novel species, and 1 candidate novel sakobuvirus species. Another kobuvirus genome represented a divergent strain of a known species. In addition, 4 divergent genomoviruses showed phylogenetic relationships with sequences reported from diverse animal and environmental sources. Notably, one candidate novel porprismacovirus (family Smacoviridae) displayed a marked discordance between its highly conserved replication-associated protein (96.7% amino acid identity), divergent capsid protein (maximum identity, 59.7%), and low whole-genome identity (63.6%). Recombination analysis suggested it might be a recombinant virus. In summary, this study expands current knowledge of the diversity and evolutionary characteristics of viruses detected in snow leopard fecal samples and provides baseline genomic data for future investigation of captive snow leopard viromes.

title: Gut microbiome profiles of two limestone forest-dwelling langurs show stronger influence of host-associated factors than environment.
authors: Xie W; Lu S; Liu Z; Zheng J; Mo F; Zhang K; Huang Z
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Host-associated factor and the environment play crucial roles in shaping the composition and function of the gut microbiome. Considerable debate exists regarding the relative influence of host-associated and environmental factors on the gut microbiome. To determine the relative importance of host-associated factors and environmental factors in langurs, we employed metagenomic sequencing to examine differences in the gut microbiome of the white-headed langurs (Trachypithecus leucocephalus) and François' langurs (T. francoisi).

RESULTS: The results revealed that the alpha diversity of the gut microbiome significantly differed between white-headed langurs and François' langurs in similar habitats. However, there was no significant variation in the alpha diversity between the wild and captive François' langurs. Similarly, the proportion of Bacillota differed between the langur species, with a higher proportion in the white-headed langurs than the François' langurs. In addition, significant separation in gut microbiome functions also occurred between the two species. The functional genes related to metabolism (e.g., carbohydrate metabolism and amino acid metabolism) and Glycoside Hydrolases in wild François' langurs were more abundant than in the other langurs. The results of PCoA showed that the pathways were significantly separated between white-headed langurs and François' langurs at four levels in the KEGG database, whereas the pathways showed no significant differences between the wild and captive François' langurs except for module level. The proportion of ARGs related to multidrug resistance was higher in wild François' langurs, likely associated with the utilization of poultry manure and antibacterial biocides in the langur's habitat.

CONCLUSION: Our study demonstrates that the host-associated factors have stronger influence on shaping the gut microbiome of langurs than environmental factors. These findings provide data on the relative contributions of host-associated factors and environmental factors to the gut microbiome of langurs and identify potential driving factors for antibiotic resistance genes. In addition, these findings provide crucial insights into the influence of host-associated factors on the gut microbiome, offering a theoretical basis for future langur conservation strategies.

title: Gut microbiome resistotypes reflect chronological age and Enterobacteriaceae relative abundance.
authors: Starikova EV; Kuzmichenko PA; Fedorov DE; Vvedensky AV; Pavlenko AV; Arkhipova AL; Kovalchuk SN; Ilina EN
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Surveillance of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in the human gut microbiota is critical for informing public health interventions and antibiotic stewardship strategies, taking into account sociodemographic, behavioral, and health-related factors. Although metagenomics research has grown exponentially, few studies have described resistome dynamics over time. In this study, we investigated resistome profiles over a 5-year interval (between 2016-2017 and 2022) in adult residents of Arkhangelsk, Northwestern Russia.

RESULTS: Over 5 years, we observed an increase in ARGs richness and abundance along with the prevalence changes in genes conferring resistance to aminoglycosides (aph2, aph3, ant9), lincosamides (lnuC), chloramphenicol (cat, catA), and macrolides (ermG, ermB). We have identified two resistotypes in our data that differed in the number of identified ARGs. The less frequent resistotype 2, characterized by a higher number of ARGs, was associated with higher participants' chronological age and increased Enterobacteriaceae abundance. Approximately one-third of the participants have shifted from one resistotype to another within a 5-year period. Temporal changes in resistome profiles occurred unevenly among participants, with the greatest changes noted for 41-45 and 61-65 age groups. No associations were found between COVID-19 history and resistome composition.

CONCLUSIONS: We showed an increase in overall ARG richness, ARG abundance, and the prevalence of certain ARGs in microbiomes of adult residents of Arkhangelsk over a 5-year period. We have identified two resistotypes; the one with higher ARGs richness was linked to higher chronological age and Enterobacteriaceae family relative abundance. These findings underscore the necessity for further antibiotic resistance surveillance to address the accelerating global dissemination of ARGs, while highlighting age as an underrecognized factor contributing to resistome dynamics.

title: Bile, sulphur and carbohydrate metabolic variation co-occur with host adiposity in mice colonized with primate microbiota.
authors: Pulvino AT; Sardaro MLS; Quinn WG; Christopher ER; Koenig S; Lucore JM; Vidal-Cruchez O; Mallott EK; Kuthyar S; Lee W; Chitta S; Gray S; Williams LE; Curley JP; Liechty ER; Ben-Sahra I; Amato KR
abstract: Although mechanistic links between the microbiome and chronic disease are increasingly well defined, how microbiomes facilitate normal variation in host metabolism remains less clear. Building on our recent demonstration that pooled faecal inocula from different primate species can cause relative differences in mouse host adiposity, we define potential mechanisms by which this could occur. Using existing samples from germ-free mice inoculated with faecal samples from humans (Homo sapiens), rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) and squirrel monkeys (Saimiri boliviensis), we integrate shotgun metagenomics of caecal contents, liquid chromatography-MS-MS metabolomics of serum and caecal contents and hepatic RNA-sequencing. Our multi-omic analysis reveals that the relative increase in adiposity previously observed in macaque-donor mice is associated with differences in hepatic cysteine catabolism and bile metabolism pathway features. These data suggest that bile and sulphur co-metabolic variation may mediate increased bile pool hydrophobicity. We also observed variation in caecal microbiome composition as well as host hepatic retinol signalling and lipid metabolism between treatments. When considered together with the observation that macaque-donor mice consumed less food than the other treatment groups, our results support the hypothesis that increased bile pool hydrophobicity results in increased dietary energy extraction. Our findings provide a foundation for future mechanistic testing of new hypotheses for understanding how the intestinal microbiomes of different primate species regulate lipid homeostasis in a mouse host.

title: Environmental gradients shape the hydrocarbon-degrading microbiome in two mid-Atlantic bays.
authors: Patabandige DLJ; John J; Ortiz M; Campbell BJ
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Hydrocarbons are recalcitrant organic matter that is released into the environment via natural and anthropogenic activities. We hypothesized that abiotic and biotic factors, including salinity, temperature, seasonality, microbial interactions, and functional redundancy, influence the abundance and activity of potential hydrocarbon degraders in the Delaware and Chesapeake Bays. We identified key genes in hydrocarbon degradation pathways in metagenomes, metatranscriptomes, and metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from these estuaries. In the surface waters of both estuaries, aerobic aromatic and alkane degradation pathways predominated, with higher gene abundances observed in low-salinity spring and summer samples. Salinity significantly structured both hydrocarbon-degrading MAG abundances, alongside temperature, nitrate, and silicate concentrations, and hydrocarbon degradation gene expression, which additionally varied seasonally, with the highest relative expression of aromatic degradation genes in low-salinity samples. Catechol degradation pathways exhibited high functional redundancy, whereas the naphthalene degradation pathway showed restricted distribution. Co-expression analysis revealed that Burkholderiales displayed condition-dependent metabolic coupling, while Pseudomonadales integrated hydrocarbon degradation with fermentation and central metabolism, demonstrating complementary strategies that support multi-scale ecosystem resilience. Together, these results support our hypothesis that environmental gradients and taxon-specific metabolic strategies jointly structure the abundance and in situ activity of hydrocarbon degraders, with implications for predicting ecosystem responses to hydrocarbon inputs under changing conditions.

IMPORTANCE: Coastal estuaries are among the most contaminated aquatic environments on Earth, receiving continuous hydrocarbon inputs from industrial activity, urban runoff, and natural sources. Microorganisms are the primary agents of hydrocarbon breakdown in these systems, yet predicting when and where this capacity is active and how resilient it is to environmental change remains a major challenge. Using paired genomic and transcriptomic data from microbial genomes across two major mid-Atlantic estuaries, we show that hydrocarbon degradation capacity is not uniformly distributed but is instead shaped by salinity, nutrients, and seasonality in pathway-specific ways. Critically, dominant degrader taxa employ fundamentally different metabolic strategies to sustain this function across fluctuating conditions, providing a form of community-level insurance against environmental disturbance. These findings advance our ability to predict microbial hydrocarbon degradation in coastal systems and inform nature-based approaches to bioremediation under increasing climate and anthropogenic pressures.

title: A metagenomic snapshot of metabolic potentials in wintertime eutrophic sediments of Lake Taihu inferred from metagenome-assembled genomes.
authors: Wei Q; Li Y; Ruan A
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Understanding the metabolic potential of microbial communities in eutrophic lake sediments at the genome-resolved level is essential for predicting nutrient cycling and stress responses in contaminated freshwater ecosystems.

METHODS: In this study, we reconstructed 206 dereplicated metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from sediment cores collected across four regions of Lake Taihu.

RESULTS: These dereplicated MAGs spanned 34 classified phyla and 72 classified genera, with 97.6% unclassified at the species level, indicating substantial genomic novelty. The cyanobacterial MAGs harbored diverse secondary metabolite biosynthetic gene clusters, suggesting a genomic basis for potential adaptive traits. Across all dereplicated MAGs, the highest biosynthetic potential for secondary metabolites was observed in Chloroflexota and Pseudomonadota. Putative antibiotic resistance genes were predominantly represented by glycopeptide resistance determinants (vanT/vanW) and resistance-nodulation-division (RND) efflux pumps, which together accounted for 86.1% of the detected resistome. Additionally, 490 predicted horizontal gene transfer (HGT) events were identified, with transferred genes being most prevalent in energy metabolism (12.4%), translation (10.8%), and transcriptional regulation (7.2%).

DISCUSSION: This genome-resolved survey provides a foundation for understanding the metabolic and genomic potential of sediment microbiomes in eutrophic freshwater systems.

title: Effects of trait stacking on the maize phyllosphere microbiome: a shotgun metagenomic comparison.
authors: Yan JY; Zhou Y; Ni L; Ding ZJ; Lin C
abstract: Current safety assessments for stacked-trait transgenic crops underrepresent the phyllosphere, a critical interface directly exposed to transgenic products, warranting strengthened risk evaluation.
