Here, we employed metagenomics to characterize the phyllosphere of three maize lines under herbicide-free conditions: wild-type (Corn.CK), herbicide-resistant single-trait (transgene of cp4-epsps, Corn.S), and insect- and herbicide-resistant stacked-trait (transgene of cry1Ab and cp4-epsps, Corn.D). Shannon diversity showed a consistent trend toward higher values in the cp4-epsps single-trait line than in the wild type (not significant after correction for multiple comparisons), whereas the stacked-trait line showed an intermediate increase. Transgenic events were associated with bidirectional taxonomic remodeling, characterized by the depletion of Enterobacterales and enrichment of environmentally adapted taxa. Functionally, transgenic lines displayed pervasive metabolic depletion across KEGG pathways and CAZyme categories, alongside reduced abundance of virulence-associated gene homologs (e.g., T6SS and Enterobactin) and lower antibiotic resistance gene diversity (wild-type > stacked-trait > single-trait), driven by the concomitant loss of Enterobacterales hosts. Notably, in most of the taxonomic, functional, virulence, and resistome dimensions examined, the stacked-trait line exhibited an intermediate microbiome profile between the wild-type and single-trait lines. These findings suggest that, for this genotype combination under these controlled conditions, trait stacking was not associated with microbiome perturbation greater than that observed for the single trait, and provide a preliminary, genotype- and stage-specific reference for phyllosphere biosafety assessment, pending field validation.

title: Genomic insight into the antibiotic-resistant determinants of Escherichia coli from small ruminants and manure in North West Province, South Africa.
authors: Howard J; Thekisoe O; Ramatla T; Lekota KE
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Livestock-associated Escherichia coli are important reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance and virulence determinants, yet comprehensive genomic data describing their genomic diversity and antibiotic resistance in South African small-ruminant production systems remain limited.

OBJECTIVE: Whole-genome sequencing was performed on 19 E. coli isolates recovered from sheep, goats, and manure collected from two farming systems in the North West Province, South Africa.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: Genomic analyses revealed a dual pattern of clonal expansion and deep heterogeneity, with globally distributed sequence types (ST10, ST155) occurring alongside several novel or rarely reported STs. Comparative genomic analyses incorporating average nucleotide identity (ANI), multilocus sequence typing (MLST), in silico serotyping, antimicrobial resistance profiling, virulence characterization, and mobile genetic element analysis revealed substantial genomic diversity, comprising globally disseminated sequence types, including ST10 and ST155, together with several novel and infrequently reported lineages.

RESULTS: Although most isolates (n =17) belonged to phylogroups A and B1, the resistome was dominated by the multidrug efflux gene mdf(A) (95%) and bla TEM - 1B (58%), corresponding with high phenotypic resistance to erythromycin (74%) and ampicillin (95%), while 26% of isolates exhibited multidrug-resistant phenotypes. Genomic analysis identified 71 plasmids representing diverse incompatibility groups and mobility classes, including conjugative and mobilizable IncHI1B and IncR plasmids carrying clinically relevant resistance genes. Approximately 89% belonged to commensal lineages (A and B1), while groups D and E were each represented by a single isolate.

CONCLUSION: To our knowledge, this represents the first whole-genome sequencing-based genomic characterization of E. coli recovered from sheep and goats in South Africa, thereby expanding the known genomic diversity of livestock-associated E. coli within the country. Furthermore, data generated in this study emphasizes the necessity of ongoing genomic monitoring to track the emergence and spread of resistant E. coli, which is crucial for monitoring and mitigating potential public health risks.

title: FAMUS: A Few-Shot Learning Framework for Large-Scale Protein Annotation.
authors: Shur G; Burstein D
abstract:
MOTIVATION: Gene function prediction is pivotal in genomic and metagenomic data analysis. Current annotation tools typically rely on the most similar sequence from the query database and struggle to robustly set meaningful hit thresholds, causing a major challenge for reliable annotation.

RESULTS: Here, we present a contrastive learning framework for functional annotation. FAMUS (Functional Annotation Method Using Supervised contrastive learning) compares query sequences to a full array of profile Hidden Markov Models, encoding each sequence's complete similarity profile, rather than only its top-scoring hit, into a condensed vector space that minimizes the distance between proteins from the same family. Unannotated sequences are incorporated as negative examples during training, enabling robust detection of proteins that fall outside the reference database without requiring user-defined thresholds. FAMUS outperformed KEGG's native KofamScan for KEGG Orthology annotation and InterPro's InterProScan for PANTHER family annotation, especially on realistic, sparsely annotated data. We used this approach to build four protein annotation models spanning the KEGG Orthology, InterPro, OrthoDB, and EggNOG databases. FAMUS is a comprehensive, modular framework that supports both pre-defined and user-specific databases. It can be readily integrated into genomic and metagenomic analysis pipelines for accurate, large-scale functional annotation.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: All four models are available as a conda package and via our web server at https://app.famus.bursteinlab.org/, and source code is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/burstein-lab/famus/ as well as a source code snapshot at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23132542.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Association of quantitative sputum Candida load with respiratory dysbiosis and airway inflammation in suspected invasive pulmonary candidiasis.
authors: Wang G; Zhang N; Peng Y; Wen X; Chen X; Zou M; Gao S; Min C; Min X; Huang J
abstract:
UNLABELLED: The clinical significance of Candida species isolation from sputum remains ambiguous due to the colonization-infection dilemma. Integrating quantitative culture with microbiome profiling may clarify its role, yet systematic evidence is scarce. In this exploratory study (June 2023-June 2026), we enrolled 140 hospitalized patients suspected of invasive pulmonary candidiasis (IPC) and stratified them into possible IPC (n = 36), probable IPC (n = 71), and negative control (n = 33) groups based on clinical criteria. All underwent quantitative fungal culture of sputum and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS). Patients were stratified by sputum Candida species load into low (<105 CFU/mL), high (≥105 CFU/mL), and negative control (0 CFU/mL) groups. We investigated associations between Candida species burden, respiratory microbiota, local inflammation (IL-8), and clinical outcomes. Higher Candida species load was significantly associated with prolonged hospitalization, elevated sputum IL-8, an increased microbial dysbiosis index, and depletion of key commensals (e.g., Neisseria, Prevotella, Rothia, Streptococcus, and Veillonella). Counterintuitively, it correlated negatively with several classic bacterial pathogens (such as Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa). A random forest model identified a nine-species microbiome signature that effectively discriminated probable from possible IPC (AUC, 0.877; 95% CI, 0.662-0.944). In patients with suspected IPC, higher sputum Candida species load is associated with exacerbated respiratory dysbiosis and airway inflammation. Quantitative Candida species assessment combined with microbiome signatures may serve as a complementary tool for stratifying disease severity and ecological disruption, meriting further validation in larger, multicenter cohorts.

IMPORTANCE: Respiratory specimens dominate clinical fungal cultures, yet interpreting the role of Candida spp. in sputum remains a diagnostic dilemma. Here, by integrating quantitative culture with metagenomic sequencing, we show that a high sputum Candida species load is a marker of profound ecological disruption. High Candida species burden was associated with significant depletion of key commensals, an elevated dysbiosis index, and heightened local inflammation. Counterintuitively, it correlated negatively with several classic bacterial pathogens, revealing a distinct dysbiotic signature. Moreover, a microbiome-based model accurately discriminated patients with probable invasive pulmonary candidiasis. Our findings suggest that quantitative sputum Candida species load, interpreted within the context of the microbial community, may be a practical biomarker for identifying patients with significant respiratory dysbiosis and inflammation, offering a path toward more refined, ecology-informed therapeutic strategies.

title: Fecal microbiota transplantation for the decolonization of mucosal adherent-invasive Escherichia coli in Crohn's disease: an open-label pilot study.
authors: Xu Z; Jiang H; Huang W; Chan A; Lin Y; Chan T; Lui RN; Wong MTL; Mak JWY; Chan FKL; Chevarin C; Colombel JF; Buisson A; Ng SC
abstract: Adherent-invasive Escherichia coli (AIEC) is implicated in Crohn's disease (CD) pathogenesis, but whether fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) clears mucosal AIEC and alters fecal and mucosal microbiomes has not been studied. In this open-label pilot study, thirty adults with CD and seropositivity for serum anti-E.coli antibody (AEcAb) received a single colonoscopic FMT from one of two donors (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT05611866). The primary outcome was adverse events (AEs) within 12 weeks after FMT; secondary outcomes included changes in mucosal AIEC, clinical measures, and fecal and mucosal microbiome profiles. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing for fecal samples and 16S rRNA sequencing for ileal mucosal samples were performed at baseline and after FMT. Baseline AEcAb levels were higher in patients with mucosal AIEC colonization (p = 0.019) and remained elevated after FMT. No FMT-related serious adverse events were reported. FMT was associated with mucosal AIEC decolonization in all 8 evaluable baseline-positive patients. Mucosal alpha diversity increased after FMT (p = 0.023), which correlated with reduced fecal calprotectin (p = 0.034). Microbial pathway profiles in CD patients resembled those of their respective donors with reduced donor-recipient dissimilarity post-FMT (p = 0.030), particularly among recipients with mucosal AIEC decolonization (p = 0.039). In conclusion, this open-label pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of FMT for modulating mucosal AIEC colonization in CD and highlights the importance of capturing microbial changes at the disease site that may be undetectable in fecal samples.

title: A central hub for convergence: multi-layer genomic networks reveal lineage-specific plasmid compatibility driving hypervirulence and carbapenem resistance in ST11 Klebsiella pneumoniae.
authors: Hai X; Wang JL; Chen Q; Lu YF; Li XP; Li CJ; Yue CF; Song JM; Yang LL; Chen M; Li HW; Zhi XY
abstract: The convergence of hypervirulence and carbapenem resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae represents a critical threat to global public health. However, the genomic mechanisms underlying this convergence, particularly the interplay between chromosomal background and mobile genetic elements, remain incompletely understood. Here, we integrated complete genome data from 102 clinical isolates from Qujing, China, with a global dataset of 4,262 genomes to construct a multi-layer population genomic framework. Using comparative genomics and sequence-similarity network analyses, we characterized the structural organization of the core genome and the population structures of plasmids and prophages. We show that the ST11 lineage serves as a central hub for the convergence of hypervirulence and carbapenem resistance. Plasmids are organized into discrete, functionally specialized communities, among which a dominant community is strongly enriched for hypervirulence and multidrug resistance determinants and preferentially associates with ST11. In contrast, the core genome exhibits a highly constrained structural organization, with most core genes embedded within conserved synteny modules, indicating strong evolutionary constraints on chromosomal architecture. Furthermore, prophages form structured yet more conserved communities that show non-random associations with plasmid types and selectively contribute to the dissemination of resistance genes. Notably, we identified a previously unreported plasmid harboring multiple copies of key virulence loci, underscoring the ongoing modular evolution of high-risk elements. Together, these findings reveal that the convergence of hypervirulence and resistance is driven by lineage-specific plasmid compatibility within a structurally constrained chromosomal background, and they establish a network-based framework for understanding the evolution of high-risk K. pneumoniae lineages.

title: Whole-genome sequencing of Lactobacillus helveticus HP-B1137 and its biotransformation capacity toward calycosin-7-O-β-D-glucoside.
authors: Zhang SH; Li LF; Fan ZS; Hou SY
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Astragalus, as a traditional tonic herb, has alycosin-7-O-β-D-glucoside as one of its main active components.

METHODS: In this study, a strain of Lactobacillus helveticus HP-B1137 was isolated from raw milk in Mudan District, Heze City, Shandong Province. The probiotic properties, and ability to biotransform calycosin-7-O-β-D-glucoside were systematically evaluated.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION: Genome analysis revealed that HP-B1137 possesses a circular chromosome (2,098,901 bp) comprising 2,161 CDs, 63 tRNAs and 12 rRNAs. Two circular plasmids were also identified, with sizes of 23,906 bp and 6,414 bp and GC contents of 38.54 and 34.49%, respectively. Functional annotation showed that the strain is rich in carbohydrate metabolism genes, with 29 glycoside hydrolase genes annotated by the CAZy database, providing a genetic basis for its glycoside-hydrolyzing capability. In vitro probiotic tests demonstrated that the strain maintained high viable cell counts after 3 min of heat treatment at 50 °C, achieved a survival rate of 108.33% after 150 min in artificial gastric juice at pH 2.7. It also inhibited 11 pathogenic bacteria, producing inhibition zones ranging from 9.83 to 16.37 mm. Whole-cell transformation experiments indicated that HP-B1137 could nearly completely convert 0.5 mg/mL calycosin-7-O-β-D-glucoside into calycosin within 36 h. Further cloning and expression of the recombinant BgsH enzyme revealed optimal reaction conditions at 37 °C and pH 7.0; under optimized conditions-0.1% substrate concentration, 10 U/mL enzyme activity, and 12-h incubation-the conversion efficiency exceeded 96.3%. In summary, L. helveticus HP-B1137 is a functional strain integrating efficient biotransformation, excellent probiotic characteristics, tolerance to extreme environments, and broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, showing significant potential for developing functional foods derived from Astragalus and green bio-manufacturing of active aglycones.

title: Genomic characteristics of a carbapenem-resistant NDM-1-producing Aeromonas caviae isolate from extraintestinal infection.
authors: Bao Z; Mao Z; Tu Y
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aims to clarify the drug resistance characteristics and genomic background of bile-derived NDM-1-producing Aeromonas caviae (A. caviae) isolate from extraintestinal infection, providing a theoretical basis for the prevention and control of clinical infections.

METHODS: A bile-derived LHL25108073-A. caviae isolate (NCBI accession number: JBSUSV000000000) was chosen as the study focus. Through flight mass spectrometry, VITEK-2 drug susceptibility phenotype validation, and whole-genome sequencing, multi-point sequence typing (MLST), VFDB database, CARD database, PlasmidFinder 2.1 software, whole-genome alignment, plasmid synteny analysis, and plasmid conjugation assay were applied for an integrative analysis.

RESULTS: This isolate was identified to be ST2281, a sequence type rarely reported across clinical, environmental, and agricultural sources, with a genome size of 4,885,524 bp and a GC content of 61.27%, carrying one chromosome (4,687,937 bp) and one drug-resistant plasmid (197,587 bp). A total of 58 high-confidence virulence genes were detected, covering common flagella, polar flagella, lateral flagella, type IV pili, Msh pili, type VI/II secretion system (T6SS/T2SS), heme-uptake systems, Endotoxins, and hemolysin, forming multiple pathogenic mechanisms. Among 14 drug resistance genes, the carbapenem-resistant NDM-1 gene was highly consistent with the genotype, only sensitive to a few drugs such as amikacin and aztreonam, based on the results of drug susceptibility tests. The drug-resistant plasmid could not autonomously conjugate and transfer due to the loss of the oriT site and was untypable by conventional plasmid typing. This plasmid shared 99-100% homology in the resistance core regions with two NDM-1-carrying A. caviae plasmids, pK433-NDM (OK287926) from sputum in Taizhou, Zhejiang, and pFAHZZU2447_NDM (CP100393) from bile in Zhengzhou, with identical bla NDM-1 sequences. Genetic background analysis based on the genomes of 157 A. caviae isolates from China and neighboring regions identified that ST313 was the dominant sequence type (ST), which accounted for the largest proportion among in Chinese isolates.

CONCLUSION: This study characterizes the molecular profiles of an extraintestinal, bile-derived NDM-1-producing A. caviae isolate belonging to ST2281, validates its abundant reservoir of virulence genes and comprehensive multi-drug resistance mechanisms, and further reveals the potential risk of NDM-1 dissemination via alternative horizontal gene transfer pathways, such as transformation and transduction. Genomic evolutionary analysis reveals that although the ST2281 isolate identified in this study shares certain phylogenetic relatedness with the prevalent ST313 lineage in China at the housekeeping gene level, whole-genome SNP-based phylogenetic analysis confirms a substantial genetic distance between them. ST2281 represents an independent and rare genetic lineage with limited global prevalence, which warrants heightened vigilance against its concealed transmission and potential clinical infection risks. Collectively, these results offer crucial genomic evidence for molecular tracing, targeted clinical antimicrobial therapy, and epidemiological containment of carbapenem resistant A. caviae.

title: ERMA: a harmonizing epicPCR data analysis tool.
authors: Dörr A; Dekić Rozman S; Duncker LV; Kehrmann J; Buer J; Virta M; Meyer F; Kraiselburd I
topics: Antimicrobial Resistance; Long-Read Microbiology; Bioinformatics Tools
abstract:
BACKGROUND: EpicPCR links functional genes to taxonomic markers at the single-cell level and has become an important method in microbial ecology and antimicrobial resistance research. However, the lack of missing standardized data analysis workflows limits reproducibility and comparability across studies. Existing analyses are often based on custom, unpublished scripts, complicating cross-study benchmarking and reuse.

RESULTS: We present ERMA, an open-source, Snakemake-based pipeline that enables an automated, standardized, reproducible, and scalable epicPCR data analysis with minimal user input. ERMA supports both Illumina and ONT sequencing data and integrates quality control, database preparation, dual similarity searches against taxonomic and functional reference databases, results integration, filtering, and visualization. The pipeline is adaptable to a broad range of research questions beyond AMR due to modular database preparation and integration of specific UniRef queries. We evaluated ERMA using five publicly available epicPCR datasets covering diverse sample sources and sequencing depths. Across these datasets, ERMA achieved mean concordance rates of approximately 70-83% with the taxonomic results reported in the respective publications. In addition, validation using a defined five-member mock community spiked into clinical wastewater demonstrated full recovery of mock genera, with 85% of ERMA-detected genera also detected by independent 16S rDNA gene analysis of the same wastewater sample. Attrition analysis showed inconsistent filtering patterns across studies, reflecting dataset-specific quality differences.

CONCLUSION: While large-scale reference datasets for epicPCR remain limited, validation using both publicly available studies and a defined mock community shows strong, interpretable performance across heterogeneous datasets. By providing a transparent, modular, and reproducible workflow, ERMA contributes toward harmonized epicPCR data analysis and establishes a foundation for future methodological standardization and benchmarking efforts as reference datasets improve.

title: Mechanism and nomenclature of methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus and implications for testing interpretation and management. A position statement on behalf of the Staphylococcus aureus working groups ISAC-SAWG and ESCMID-ESGS.
authors: Saeed K; Mason-Slingerland BCGC; David MZ; Stefani S; Stegger M; Vos MC; Skov RL
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Beyond mec-mediated resistance, Staphylococcus aureus has developed complex resistance mechanisms against anti-staphylococcal β-lactam-antibiotics. The scientific community lacks a unified consensus on the nomenclature/clinical implications of these mechanisms.

OBJECTIVES: This position statement by members of Staphylococcus Working Groups of the International Society of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy and the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases proposes a set of names for various types of methicillin/oxacillin reduced susceptibility/resistance in S. aureus.

CONTENT: The Working Groups propose the following categorisation: (1) Mec-mediated methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA): This is due to mec (mecA or mecB or mecC) mediated resistance. They can exhibit heteroresistant expression to methicillin. (2) Methicillin-resistant S. aureus lacking mec (MRLM): Isolates are cefoxitin and/or oxacillin resistant but mec-negative, and do not show heteroresistance. They can be subdivided into 2a) hyperproduction of β-lactamase and 2b) modifications of natural penicillin-binding-proteins (PBP). Importantly, these mechanisms cannot easily be differentiated in routine laboratories. If the resistance mechanism is not fully characterised we suggest using the name methicillin-resistant lacking mec (MRLM). Isolates with hyperproduction of β-lactamase show low-level resistance to oxacillin, but most isolates test susceptible to cefoxitin. When the mechanism is characterised we propose they should be named hyper-beta-lactamase-producing-S. aureus (HBSA) instead of the hitherto used term borderline oxacillin-resistant S. aureus (BORSA). Isolates with resistance due to modifications of the PBP 1-4 in S. aureus, we propose to continue to name these modified S. aureus (MODSA). MODSA isolates in routine diagnostic laboratories most commonly present as cefoxitin-resistant. (3) Oxacillin susceptible-mec-positive S. aureus (OS-MRSA). Strains carry a mec gene, but harbor mutations, deletions or insertion rendering them phenotypically susceptible to oxacillin/cefoxitin.

IMPLICATIONS: The proposed changes clarify methicillin resistance nomenclature in S. aureus, removing current ambiguity from clinical communication and literature. As novel methicillin resistance mechanisms emerge in S. aureus, the definition must be updated accordingly.

title: Serotype-independent inhibition of S. pneumoniae by SMiTE, a commensal-derived bacteriocin.
authors: Lança J; Bryton J; Borralho J; Candeias C; Antunes W; Pandi A; Sá-Leão R
abstract: Streptococcus pneumoniae remains a leading cause of disease despite widespread vaccination, highlighting the need for serotype-independent strategies. We recently identified commensal streptococci that produce bacteriocins with anti-pneumococcal activity. Here, we evaluate these bacteriocins as candidates for pneumococcal control. Using cell-free protein synthesis, we screened 58 bacteriocins, the majority of which absent in available pneumococcal genomes, and identified SMiTE as the most potent. Purified SMiTE disrupted pneumococcal membrane integrity, as shown by confocal, transmission, and scanning electron microscopy, induced ATP leakage, and triggered transcriptional responses consistent with envelope stress and metabolic remodeling. In a mouse nasopharyngeal colonization model, intranasal SMiTE treatments reduced pneumococcal loads by 65-fold with no significant weight loss. SMiTE inhibited a broad range of serotypes, with the strongest activity against serotype 3, which is poorly controlled by current vaccines, while sparing most oral and upper respiratory tract commensals. Repeated sub-inhibitory exposure did not select resistant mutants in line with the membrane-targeting mechanism. These findings establish SMiTE as a commensal-derived strategy for serotype-independent, microbiota-sparing pneumococcal decolonization.IMPORTANCEStreptococcus pneumoniae is a bacterium that can cause serious infections such as pneumonia, meningitis, and bloodstream infections. Although vaccines have greatly reduced disease, they do not protect against all strains, making new approaches urgently needed. In this study, we discovered a natural antimicrobial molecule, called SMiTE, produced by harmless bacteria that normally live in the human mouth. SMiTE effectively kills pneumococci by damaging their protective membrane, preventing them from surviving. In mice, a simple nasal treatment with SMiTE dramatically reduced the amount of pneumococci in the nose, where these bacteria first establish themselves before spreading or causing disease. Importantly, SMiTE was active against many different pneumococcal strains, including serotype 3, which is poorly controlled by current vaccines, while leaving most beneficial bacteria unharmed. Because it did not readily trigger resistance, SMiTE represents a promising new strategy to prevent pneumococcal carriage, transmission, and disease, regardless of serotype.

title: Adaptive landscape of the metallo-β-lactamase NDM-1 to emerging β-lactam-based therapies.
authors: Romero FD; Drusin SI; Bahr G; González G; Bonomo RA; Moreno DM; González LJ; Vila AJ
abstract: The New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM) is a major determinant of carbapenem resistance. This has prompted the development of novel therapeutic strategies to treat NDM producers. Since these therapies impose new selective pressures, their clinical deployment may favor NDM variants carrying escape mutations. To anticipate these events and inform therapeutic decisions, we explored the evolutionary landscape of NDM-1 under different selective constraints. To this end, we generated a diverse library of blaNDM variants and challenged it with zinc starvation, antibiotics, or β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations that represent novel and emerging therapies. Selection under zinc limitation and cefotaxime identified mutational trajectories that recapitulate clinical NDM evolution, validating the diversity of the library and its predictive nature. Drug-specific selections revealed sharply different evolutionary pathways. Mecillinam selected a narrow evolutionary pathway centered on residues N220 and M67, which enhance productive active-site interactions with this penicillin. Cefepime/taniborbactam selected multiple escape routes, dominated by substitutions at E152 and, secondarily, K211, that impair productive interaction with taniborbactam. In contrast, cefiderocol/xeruborbactam under iron-depleted conditions and aztreonam/avibactam did not select NDM variants conferring an improved resistance phenotype in the tested Escherichia coli background. These results show that NDM evolution is constrained by the chemistry of each therapeutic challenge. Substrate adaptation is possible for mecillinam, inhibitor escape is readily accessible for taniborbactam, whereas no NDM-centered escape was detected for the aztreonam- and xeruborbactam-based conditions tested. Mapping drug-specific NDM-centered landscapes can identify therapies that readily select enzyme-level escape and those for which resistance is more likely to require mechanisms beyond blaNDM sequence variation.IMPORTANCECarbapenem-resistant infections by Enterobacterales are increasingly difficult to treat because bacteria can destroy some of the most powerful antibiotics used in the clinic. This study focuses on Escherichia coli carrying variants of the New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM), an enzyme that enables bacteria to resist carbapenem antibiotics. New therapies are being developed to overcome this problem, but bacteria may evolve again when exposed to these treatments. Here, we tested how New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase can adapt under the evolutionary pressure of last-resort therapies. The results show that not all treatments carry the same evolutionary risk. Some drugs allow the enzyme to adapt through specific mutations, whereas other combinations did not yield improved NDM variants in the tested bacterial background. This work identifies which treatments readily select changes within NDM and which may require resistance mechanisms elsewhere in the bacterial cell. These findings should be integrated with host species, permeability, drug targets, metal uptake, and co-produced enzymes when considering clinical resistance.

title: MtbAIM: AI/ML-guided endpoint-specific prediction of small-molecule activity across drug-susceptible and drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis
authors: Singh, J.; Singh, K.
abstract: The emergence of drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb) presents a major challenge to drug discovery, as compounds active against drug-susceptible (DS) isolates may not retain comparable inhibitory activity against drug-resistant (DR) isolates. Here, we developed an AI/ML workflow to independently prioritize small molecules separately against DS and DR isolates of M.tb and predict MIC, MIC90, and MIC99 as distinct quantitative endpoints. Following curation of data retrieved from the ChEMBL repository, molecular-activity datasets comprised 25,645 and 3,749 compounds tested against whole cell DS and DR isolates respectively. Molecular representations were generated using RDKit descriptors and Morgan fingerprints, along with embeddings from ChemBERTa, MolCLR, and Uni-Mol, and evaluated for binary activity classification and endpoint-specific regression. The best-performing DS classifier combined RDKit/Morgan features with ExtraTrees (balanced accuracy 0.782; AUROC 0.864; AUPRC 0.870), while histogram gradient boosting using the same features performed best for DR classification (balanced accuracy 0.762; AUROC 0.836; AUPRC 0.880). Similarly, RDKit/Morgan features combined with tree-based regressors achieved the best overall performance across all six DS/DR regression endpoints, with pooled out-of-fold RMSE values ranging from 0.604 to 0.784 pMIC units. To facilitate broader application, we developed MtbAIM (https://github.com/jasdeep002/MtbAIM), a Google Colab-based prediction platform that enables users to assess and prioritize small molecules against DS and DR isolates of M.tb.

title: tRNAZAP: Deep learning toolkit for nanopore tRNA signal analysis
authors: Daneshwar Kakhaki, P.; Akeson, S.; Ghohabi Esfahani, N.; Abu-Shumays, R. L.; Jain, M.
abstract: tRNA are short, ~76 nucleotide-long, modification-rich molecules that play an important role in protein translation. Nanopore sequencing is the only platform capable of directly sequencing full-length, native tRNA molecules. This capability is enabled by splinted ligation of tRNA-specific adapters. As a result, the measured ionic current signal reflects a composition of both adapter and tRNA sequence features. Despite these advantages, analysis of nanopore tRNA sequencing data poses distinct computational challenges. Existing ionic current-based signal-to-sequence decoding (basecalling) models are optimized for mRNA and perform suboptimally on short, modification-dense RNA such as tRNA. Furthermore, alignment algorithms for reference-guided analysis of short-length reads are not optimized for nanopore reads with lower accuracy than Next-generation sequencing reads. To overcome these limitations, domain-specific computational approaches are required. We present tRNAZAP, a nanopore ionic current signal analysis toolkit designed to enable precise reference-guided sequence alignment. tRNAZAP operates directly on raw ionic current signals and decomposes the analysis into two complementary tasks: 1) segmentation of adapter and tRNA regions, and 2) tRNA classification, both implemented using transformer-based models. The segmentation component isolates the tRNA signal portion and extracts the corresponding nucleotide sequence as the alignment query, while the classification component identifies the tRNA type as the alignment reference without requiring sequence-level information. Together, these outputs allow direct optimal pairwise alignment between the tRNA subsequence of the full query and reference sequences. Trained on in vitro transcribed RNA data and evaluated on yeast tRNA, these models achieved ~98% classification accuracy and intersection-over-union of ~0.98 for segmentation.

title: Unsupervised decomposition of massively parallel TraDIS-Xpress fitness data from  Escherichia coli  identifies distinct functional and expression modules of antimicrobial resistance determinants
authors: Yasir, M.; Turner, A. K.; Telatin, A.; Bastkowski, S.; Holden, E. R.; Charles, I. G.; Webber, M. A.
abstract: Linking genotype to phenotype is a central goal in biology, one way to do this is using transposon insertion sequencing (TIS) where the fitness impacts of mutations across a genome are assessed in different conditions. Traditional analyses use comparison of each gene response independently in control versus test conditions, so a compendium of hundreds of test conditions returns hundreds of separate ranked gene lists. To unlock the potential information hidden within large data sets, we applied independent component (ICA) analysis to 754 Escherichia coli BW25113 TraDIS-Xpress samples. These samples included a series of antibiotic and other stress condition exposures. ICA is designed to identify hidden structure within complex data and to extract meaningfully linked components. In this analysis each annotated gene was resolved into a gene body and 198 bp 5' and 3' features so that expression effects driven by the transposon's outwards facing promoter enter the matrix separately from gene disruption effects. The decomposition returned 99 components, which we term fxModules, which were defined as containing elements with similar responses across the whole compendium rather than per any individual experiment. Of the 754 stress samples, the antibiotic arm included 110 samples derived from exposure to 14 separate agents at multiple concentrations. Many of these have been highly studied allowing us to explore the accuracy of predicted responsive fxModules. This analysis showed excellent predictive power of the approach and the fxModules responsive to individual drugs typically reproduced known mechanisms at a resolution superior to analysis of single gene sets. For example, exposure to fosfomycin identified responsive fxModules containing genes which are known to be involved in uptake of the drug, cAMP-CRP control and exposure to gentamicin identified oxidative phosphorylation split across three fxModules responding with different magnitudes and directions at different concentrations. This recapitulates recent work studying the landscape of E. coli genes sensitive to this drug with high precision without any prior knowledge of functional annotation. Similarly precise predictions were made for other drugs. Responsive modules also identified novel groups of genes and linkages beyond the boundaries of defined pathways as being responsive to various stresses demonstrating the ability to predict new genotype-phenotype links. Inclusion of the regulatory regions also resolved fxModules which were entirely contributed by promoter regions, for example for chloramphenicol genes responsible for efflux were identified by signals in intergenic control regions, and unidirectional insertions in gene bodies, a signal that a gene level matrix would not be able to predict with accuracy. These data show that ICA decomposition provides an efficient and accurate annotation independent approach to identifying sets of genes with related functional impacts in any given condition in the compendium. The functional modular association of genes also help in predicting gene functions of unknown genes based on the group function. This approach allows rapid identification of novel genotype-phenotype links and unlocks the power of multiple comparisons of transposon mutagenesis data.

title: Ethnic differences in gut microbiota composition and functional capacity persist over six years in the HELIUS multi-ethnic longitudinal cohort
authors: Verhaar, B. J. H.; Boulund, U.; Herrema, H.; Nicolaou, M.; Zwinderman, A. H.; van den Born, B.-J. H.; Hamdiui, N.; Elinav, E.; Nielsen, T.; Nieuwdorp, M.
abstract: Background: Ethnic minority groups in Western Europe carry a disproportionate cardiometabolic disease burden not fully explained by conventional risk factors, and their gut microbiomes differ markedly from those of European-origin populations. Whether these differences persist over time has not been examined prospectively. Results: We followed 1,903 participants from six ethnic groups in the HELIUS cohort over 6 years, using faecal 16S rRNA sequencing across all groups and shotgun metagenomics in a matched Dutch and South-Asian Surinamese subset (N = 238 per group). The extent of microbiota compositional change over time differed between ethnic groups: Moroccan participants showed the largest change, while the Dutch and South-Asian Surinamese participants were most stable. Diabetes mellitus and medication use at baseline were associated with greater compositional drift. However, ethnic differences in composition were largely preserved across all six groups (16S: ethnicity R2 0.044 to 0.037; all 15 pairwise contrasts significant at follow-up) and in the shotgun subset (R2 0.047 to 0.037). At the species level, 61 of 78 ethnicity-associated species remained differentially abundant at follow-up. Alistipes putredinis, the species converging most strongly, was absent at baseline in 43% of South-Asian Surinamese participants, and the convergence was consistent with acquisition of this species by this group. At strain level, within-person strain sharing declined with follow-up duration but was similar between ethnic groups. Within hosts, 90% of A. putredinis populations were retained as the same or a closely related lineage, and within the retained subset, microdiversity increased in both groups. Ethnic differences in functional profiles persisted to a similar extent as those in composition, with limited convergence in fibre-degrading enzyme families (GH5_37, GH26). The total antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) burden in the gut microbiome declined similarly in both groups over time. Dutch participants showed higher baseline ARG diversity that converged toward South-Asian Surinamese levels, while class-level differences were predominantly stable. Conclusions: Six years of follow-up in a shared urban environment narrowed ethnic differences in the gut microbiome only modestly; assuming exponential decline, the observed change corresponds to a half-life of roughly two decades.

title: Isoindole-benzohydrazide derivative potentiates colistin activity to overcome resistance conferred by MCR-1 variants in Escherichia coli
authors: Wolf, A. S.; Ndupu, R. O.; Alumasa, J. N.
abstract: Polymyxin antibiotic resistance mediated by the mobilized colistin resistance (MCR) enzyme threatens the last-resort treatment of deadly multidrug-resistant pathogens, including Acinetobacter baumannii, and calls for urgent mitigation efforts. We used a multifaceted approach involving computational and wet-lab techniques to identify an isoindole-benzohydrazide derivative, JNAL-042, which potentiates colistin activity in an Escherichia coli MCR-resistance phenotype screening model. JNAL-042 lacked intrinsic antibiotic activity but potentiated that of polymyxin antibiotics at 12-24 mug/ml, as demonstrated by bacterial growth susceptibility screens. Cell viability counts and time-kill assays corroborated these findings, demonstrating complete abolition of MCR-mediated resistance by the antibiotic-adjuvant combination at concentrations mirroring those of empty vector controls. Post-induction treatment with this combination similarly prevented the propagation of the resistance phenotype, albeit at a higher antibiotic dose. This landmark study presents JNAL-042 as a promising antibiotic adjuvant to combat MCR-mediated resistance and offers a viable solution to preserve last-resort polymyxin antibiotics.

title: From dynamic transcripts to stable proteins: multi-omics revealed regulatory buffering of Candidatus Accumulibacter under cyclic conditions
authors: Pei, R.; Cardona, L.; Rodilla Ramirez, P. N.; Singh Saini, J.; Stephanie Willemin, M.; Pavlou, M. P.; Holliger, C.
abstract: Enhanced biological phosphorus removal (EBPR) relies on polyphosphate-accumulating organisms that experience dynamic fluctuations in redox conditions and substrate availability. How these organisms regulate metabolism across molecular layers under cyclic operation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated molecular regulation in a long-term, stable aerobic granular sludge system dominated by Candidatus Accumulibacter. We combined metagenomics, time-resolved metatranscriptomics, and matched metaproteomics across three consecutive operational cycles. Genome-resolved metagenomics revealed an Accumulibacter-dominated community encoding canonical EBPR functions. Time-resolved metatranscriptomics revealed extensive and reproducible transcriptional dynamics affecting hundreds of genes. These dynamics did not align with discrete EBPR phases or instantaneous environmental transitions, but instead unfolded gradually over the cycle. Despite pronounced transcript-level heterogeneity, aggregation at the functional level revealed strong consolidation, with only a limited number of KEGG orthologs exhibiting coherent temporal regulation. Quantitative metaproteomics revealed a stable proteome across EBPR cycles, with no individual proteins or functional categories showing significant differential abundance despite direct transcript-protein mapping and time-matched sampling. This indicated that transcriptional dynamics did not translate into measurable changes in protein pool size on the time scale of individual cycles, consistent with slow, growth-coupled proteome turnover relative to cycle duration. Together, these results support a hierarchical model of regulation in Candidatus Accumulibacter, in which dynamic transcriptional responses are buffered at both the functional and protein levels. This organization provides a plausible basis for stable EBPR performance under predictable cyclic operation and demonstrates how time-resolved multi-omics can be used to resolve regulatory dynamics across molecular layers in engineered microbial ecosystems.

title: Mechanistic prediction of fecal microbiota transplant engraftment and Clostridioides difficile colonization resistance with μODE
authors: Cumbo, F.; Joshi, J.; Raubenolt, B.; Katzenmeyer, N.; Claesen, J.; Blankenberg, D.
abstract: Shotgun metagenomics routinely resolves microbial community composition down to the strain level via metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), but translating these static catalogs into mechanistic, time-resolved understandings of ecosystem dynamics remains a critical computational bottleneck. Here, we present muODE, a fully automated framework that converts MAGs into dynamical simulations of community metabolism equipped with a composable, literature-grounded ecology layer, fundamentally designed to serve as a mechanistic hypothesis-testing engine. It employs dynamic flux balance analysis (dFBA) coupled to a shared extracellular pool and integrates a composable ecology layer capturing pH inhibition, time-varying antibiotic pharmacokinetics, bile-acid transformations, and spore dormancy. To evaluate the core engine, we cross-validated the dFBA machinery to machine precision against an independent reference implementation. We provide native export to the established COMETS engine for third-party verification. Benchmarking against two independent experimentally validated datasets confirmed that while monoculture growth is robustly captured, overflow secretion and directed community composition remain strictly bounded by the flux-routing limitations of max-biomass FBA. However, when applied to rate-modifying ecological feedback, muODE mechanistically and quantitatively reproduces bile-acid-mediated colonization resistance against Clostridioides difficile. With a single rate parameter calibrated so that baseline deoxycholate matched its measured physiological concentration, the framework reproduced the uncalibrated antibiotic-induced collapse of deoxycholate, with the calibrated inhibitor concentration coinciding with the independently set inhibitory threshold of the pathogen and driving a ~44x shift in the simulated pathogen-susceptibility ratio; bile-acid transformation is represented in the composable ecology layer rather than in the genome-scale stoichiometry. Finally, applying muODE end-to-end to a real longitudinal fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) yielding 139 de novo genome-scale metabolic models, the framework successfully recovered the clinical direction of treatment. By transparently diagnosing the structural competitive-exclusion bias that limits precise compositional prediction, muODE motivates the necessity of community-objective extensions while transitioning microbiome modeling from descriptive taxonomy toward testable, quantitatively-validated dynamic hypothesis testing, laying the essential mechanistic groundwork for the predictive engineering of safe, targeted ecological therapeutics. muODE is freely available at https://github.com/cumbof/muODE.

title: Assessment of antimicrobial potential of cell-free supernatant from Lacticaseibacillus paracasei SRG isolated from the vaginal microbiota of healthy women against uropathogens
authors: Anand, R.; Rai, D.; Prakash, P.; Maurya, G. K.
abstract: Among women, urinary tract infection (UTI) represents a major health concern. Approximately 50% of the adult female population experienced an episode of UTI at least once. UTI and recurrent UTIs caused by resistant bacteria are very common in clinical settings. The treatment and management of UTI is becoming more challenging because of the rise in antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Lactobacillus spp are the dominant bacterial genus in urinary and vaginal microbiota, which are also used as probiotics. In this study, Lacticaseibacillus paracasei SRG isolated from the vagina of healthy women were evaluated for its probiotic-associated properties and cell-free supernatant (CFS)-mediated antibacterial activity against eight uropathogens. The antibacterial activity of CFS was concentration- and pH-dependent, which was significantly evident at CFS/2 and CFS/4 concentrations and acidic pH values of 4 and 5. The antibacterial activity in CFS remains unaltered even after heat and proteinase K treatment, which suggests the role of heat- and protease-resistant metabolites beside the contributions from acidic conditions. L. paracasei SRG showed strong autoaggregation (85.32%) and cell-surface hydrophobicity (55.60%). In addition, it also exhibits co-aggregation with all indicator strains, suggesting substantial interaction with diverse pathogenic bacteria. These observations highlighted the L. paracasei SRG as a potential probiotic candidate developed from indigenous vaginal microbiota.

title: Exploring recurrent urinary tract infection: paired microbiota and culture-based profiling reveals stable dysbiosis and multidrug-resistant, virulence-enriched uropathogens
authors: Kaushik, S.; P, K.; Pal, S.; Nandi, N.; Kiran, G. S.; Kumar, S. H. K.; Selvin, J.; Veettil, V. N.; Devi, S.
abstract: **Objectives:** Recurrent urinary tract infection (rUTI) is increasingly complicated by antimicrobial resistance (AMR), yet urinary microbiome dysbiosis and isolate-level resistance-virulence are rarely examined together across different treatment states. In this study, we characterized both within the same sample in rUTI and in healthy controls. **Methods:** In this cross-sectional cohort, mid-stream urine was collected from women with untreated, treated and prophylaxis rUTI and age-matched healthy controls at four centres in South India. Of 80 samples collected, 75 were analysed (26 controls, 20 untreated, 20 treated, 9 prophylaxis) by 16S rRNA V3-V4 sequencing. In addition, 105 culturable isolates from the same samples were identified and tested for antimicrobial susceptibility (VITEK 2) and phenotypic virulence. **Results:** rUTI groups showed approximately half the alpha diversity of controls (median Shannon 1.07-1.18 vs 2.17; Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.041). Community structure differed from controls in every rUTI subgroup (PERMANOVA R-squared = 0.091, p = 0.004; pairwise FDR = 0.008) but not among subgroups. Mean Lactobacillus relative abundance fell from 29.2% in controls to <=13.2% in rUTI groups, while Escherichia-Shigella rose from 7.2% to 25.0-43.0%. Control-referenced dysbiosis z-scores were elevated in all rUTI groups (community distance: FDR <= 0.003; uropathogen: Lactobacillus index: FDR < 0.001 for treated and prophylaxis groups). Among isolates, Escherichia coli predominated (35/105; 16/35, 45.7% multidrug-resistant), followed by Klebsiella spp. (32% multidrug-resistant); carbapenem susceptibility was largely retained, and multidrug-resistant E. coli co-carried more virulence traits. **Conclusions:** rUTI is associated with a stable dysbiotic state that treatment does not restore, combining Lactobacillus loss and uropathogen dominance with a multidrug-resistant culturable reservoir that co-accumulates virulence traits. Reading the community and its isolates together may support microbiome-sparing, resistance-aware management of rUTI.

title: Structure-Based Drug Design of Novel Inhibitors Targeting the Thiamine Biosynthesis Pathway in Bacteria
authors: Krishna, N.; Ulaganathan, V.
abstract: Current generation antibiotics are limited by poor target selectivity and are often mismanaged, leading to widespread antimicrobial resistance. The bacterial thiamine biosynthesis pathway offers compelling alternative since it is highly essential for bacterial survival and yet absent in humans. Genetic perturbations within pathway lead to documented auxotrophy and virulence defects, indicating low mutational tolerance within this pathway. Thiamine phosphate synthase is a key bottleneck enzyme performing the crucial role of coupling thiazole and pyrimidine moieties to form thiamine monophosphate. To develop a suitable inhibitor against it, a structure-based drug design pipeline was implemented. High-throughput virtual screening of nearly 1.5 million molecules provided sufficient exploration of chemical space. Further, R-group substitution was utilized for lead optimization. Structure-Activity Relationship analysis upon molecular mutants reveals patterns among R-group interactions to catalytic residues across various scaffolds. Additionally, ADMET screening and validation using molecular dynamics simulations resulted in a potent orally bioavailable broad-spectrum bactericidal molecule.

title: Gain-of-function mutations in the RodZ juxtamembrane domain promote Rod system activity in Escherichia coli
authors: Suarez, K. A.; Bernhardt, T.
abstract: The peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall protects bacteria from osmotic lysis and determines their shape. In rod-shaped bacteria, the lateral wall is elongated by the Rod system (elongasome). This synthetic machine is built around the RodA-PBP2 PG synthase complex, the actin-like protein MreB, and the accessory proteins MreC, MreD, and RodZ. Notably, RodZ shares a similar domain organization with FtsN, an essential division protein that triggers PG synthesis by the division apparatus (divisome). Both are single pass transmembrane proteins that bind actin-like proteins in the cytoplasm and have largely unstructured periplasmic regions capped by small, folded C-terminal domains. We therefore investigated whether RodZ might function like FtsN in activating the Rod system. To this end, gain-of-function variants of Escherichia coli RodZ were isolated that restored growth and shape to cells producing a hypomorphic mreC mutant. Production of these RodZ variants in wild-type cells increased resistance to the MreB antagonist A22 and enhanced sensitivity to the beta-lactam mecillinam. These phenotypes have all previously been associated with Rod system hyperactivation, and we found that they were caused by substitutions in the cytoplasmic juxtamembrane (JM) domain of RodZ. This domain is analogous to the N-terminus of FtsN known to promote divisome activation via its interaction with filaments of the actin-like FtsA protein. Structural modeling indicates that the JM domain of RodZ is similarly likely to associate with MreB filaments. Our results therefore support a model in which RodZ activates PG synthesis by the Rod system via a mechanism analogous to divisome activation by FtsN.

title: NanoPlasmiQC: Full plasmid sequencing with ONT long-reads and automatic data analysis
authors: de Oliveira, J. A. V. S.; Ng, V.; Wolff, K.; Pucker, B.
abstract: Long-read sequencing has shown a rapid technological development during the last years. It has been established as the standard method for the sequencing of plant genomes and has also gained importance for full plasmid sequencing. As Sanger sequencing has a limited read length of about 1 kb, long read sequencing offers a great advantage, as the full plasmid can be sequenced in one read. Here, we present a cost-effective workflow to sequence full plasmids and compare the results against an expectation. The per plasmid cost of this workflow is determined by the number of plasmids investigated simultaneously, but can be lower than the price of a single Sanger sequencing reaction. We developed a workflow for automatic data processing, which allows us to complete sequencing and data analysis within a day.

title: Disruption of cAMP Signalling and RNA Regulation Confers Cefiderocol Resistance in Acinetobacter baumannii
authors: De Oliveira, D. M. P.; Heaton, R.; Whyte, H.; Buedenbender, L.; Indraratna, A.; Nguyen, N. T. K.; Phan, M.-D.; Alquethamy, S. F.; Hirose, Y.; Permana, B.; Wright, A.; Peleg, A. Y.; Nochomovitz, M.; Harris, P. N. A.; Ramsay, K. A.; Holmes, P.; Blaskovich, M. A. T.; Paterson, D. L.; Boyce, J. D.; Everest-Dass, A.; Schembri, M. A.; Tree, J. J.; Walker, M. J.; Forde, B. M.
abstract: Cefiderocol is a siderophore-conjugated cephalosporin used to treat severe multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections. Its recent prioritisation for US national preparedness underscores its clinical importance, yet resistance can emerge despite apparent in vitro susceptibility. Here, we identify two regulatory routes to cefiderocol resistance in carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB): mutation of the cAMP-producing adenylate cyclase CavA and truncation of the glycine-rich RNA-binding domain of the post-transcriptional regulator Hfq. These variants occurred in contemporary clinical isolates, conferred resistance in a murine CRAB lung-infection model and imposed minimal fitness costs. In Escherichia coli, deletion of the CavA orthologue cyaA increased competitive fitness during sub-inhibitory cefiderocol exposure. Hfq-CLASH and integrated omics revealed Hfq-dependent regulation of Fur-associated iron homeostasis in A. baumannii. Under iron limitation, truncated-Hfq induced a defence-primed state that attenuated siderophore uptake and reduced cefiderocol activity. These findings identify bacterial regulatory state and iron availability as determinants of cefiderocol susceptibility, with implications for resistance surveillance and susceptibility testing.

title: Pharmacokinetics and Efficacy of the FimH Inhibitor Sibofimloc in Preventing Necrotizing Enterocolitis in Preterm Piglets
authors: Melendez Hebib, V.; Earls, B.; Stoll, B.; Vonderohe, C.; Guthrie, G.; Haiser, H. J.; Paton, M.; Balani, S.; Hesse, M.; Burrin, D.
abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a disease in preterm infants associated with an increased abundance of Enterobacteriaceae. FimH, a mannose-binding adhesin on Enterobacteriaceae type 1 fimbriae, mediates mucosal attachment and TLR4-dependent inflammatory cascades. We evaluated the safety, pharmacokinetics, and efficacy of an oral FimH inhibitor (Sibofimloc) to reduce Enterobacteriaceae colonization and prevent NEC in preterm piglets. We performed a 9-d dose-escalation safety study (10, 25, 50 mg/kg BID) assessing absorption and tolerability and a 10-d randomized efficacy study. Piglets in the efficacy study received an infant formula diet with or without oral sibofimloc (40 mg/kg BID), or donor human milk (DHM) as a healthy control. NEC incidence, tissue histopathology, and gut microbiota composition via metagenomic whole-genome sequencing (WGS) were evaluated. Systemic exposure data reveal that sibofimloc was dose-dependently absorbed, while plasma levels decreased from postnatal day 2 to day 8, indicating reduced drug absorption with maturation of the intestinal barrier. Treatment with sibofimloc did not reduce NEC incidence (100% in sibofimloc in formula controls) or severity, whereas DHM-fed piglets experienced 0% NEC. Sibofimloc-treated animals exhibited significantly reduced crypt depths, demonstrating heightened mucosal injury and impaired regenerative capacity. WGS revealed that sibofimloc-treated animals maintained a gut luminal microbiota composition similar to untreated formula controls, dominated by Clostridium perfringens (C. perfringens). Selective targeting of FimH-expressing Enterobacteriaceae was insufficient to prevent NEC or alter the gut microbiota in this preterm piglet model, underscoring the complexity of NEC-associated microbial communities and suggesting that additional microbial targets and other colonization mechanisms may contribute to disease development.

title: Allyl chloride respiration by Dehalobacter shapes the fate of 1,2,3-trichloropropane
authors: Wang, X.; Zhang, Y.; Wang, H.; Capiro, N. L.; Yu, L.; Xiu, Z.; Li, Q.; Manefield, M.; Loffler, F. E.; Yan, H.; Sun, W.; Yang, Y.
abstract: The synthetic compound 1,2,3-trichloropropane (1,2,3-TCP) is a persistent groundwater contaminant and probable human carcinogen for which effective detoxification pathways remain limited. Under anoxic conditions, microbial transformation of 1,2,3-TCP typically stalls at the intermediate allyl chloride, preventing complete detoxification. Here, we report the enrichment and characterization of Dehalobacter restrictus strain XRTCP, a bacterium capable of coupling dichloroelimination of 1,2,3-TCP with subsequent hydrogenolysis of allyl chloride to propene. While dichloroelimination to allyl chloride has been previously observed, the ability to utilize allyl chloride as a respiratory electron acceptor represents a previously unrecognized metabolic capability. This transformation was linked to microbial growth, with cell densities increasing by up to 74-fold during 1,2,3-TCP reduction and 15.8-fold during allyl chloride transformation. Metagenomic and metaproteomic analyses revealed a diverse repertoire of reductive dehalogenases (RDases), with expression patterns that differed between 1,2,3-TCP and allyl chloride amendments. Notably, a tcpA-like RDase was expressed under both 1,2,3-TCP and allyl chloride conditions, while distinct RDases were preferentially expressed under each substrate, indicating functional specialization within the dechlorination pathway. Despite this metabolic capability, propene formation remained limited due to rapid abiotic transformation of allyl chloride, primarily via reactions with reduced sulfur species, highlighting a critical branching point between biotic and abiotic pathways. These findings demonstrate that allyl chloride can function as a growth-supporting respiratory electron acceptor. More broadly, this work reveals how interactions between microbial metabolism and geochemical processes govern contaminant fate, with implications for improving both monitored natural attenuation and engineered bioremediation strategies for chlorinated solvents.

title: Bacteriophage susceptibility in clinical Enterococcus faecalis reflects host genomic background and Epa-associated phage adsorption
authors: Nakamura, T.; Fujiki, J.; AlcHepNet Investigators,; Schnabl, B.
abstract: Cytolysin-positive Enterococcus faecalis has been implicated as a disease-associated pathobiont in alcohol-associated hepatitis, motivating development of selective bacteriophage-based strategies. However, strain-level determinants of phage susceptibility remain incompletely understood. We characterized the host range of three E. faecalis phages, {Phi}Ef2.1, {Phi}Ef2.2, and {Phi}Ef2.3Ev, across 45 clinical isolates and investigated bacterial and phage factors associated with adsorption and productive infection. Isolates were characterized by whole-genome sequencing, cytolysin status, antimicrobial resistance determinants, and predicted anti-phage defense systems. Phage susceptibility was measured by efficiency of plating (EoP) and adsorption assays. Thirty-five of the 45 isolates (77.8%), including all 15 cylLs-positive isolates, were susceptible to at least one of the three phages at EoP [≥]0.01. {Phi}Ef2.1 and {Phi}Ef2.2 showed greater activity against cylLs-positive isolates, which also carried higher burdens of predicted antimicrobial resistance determinants and anti-phage defense system types. Analysis of 367 complete E. faecalis RefSeq genomes classified the variable region of the enterococcal polysaccharide antigen (epa) locus into 15 recurrent architecture groups that were associated with phage-specific adsorption patterns. Efficient adsorption did not always result in productive infection, indicating additional post-adsorption barriers. AbiD emerged as a candidate factor associated with reduced {Phi}Ef2.2 productivity, although this signal was prediction-tool dependent, while unexplained post-adsorption blocks suggest the involvement of additional uncharacterized mechanisms. These findings link naturally occurring epa architecture to phage adsorption and highlight distinct post-adsorption constraints on host range, providing a framework for rational phage selection against clinically relevant E. faecalis populations.

title: Root exudates enhance the ecological fitness of a non-native PGPR and reshape rhizosphere microbiome assembly
authors: Mondal, S.; Roy, D.; Bhattacharya, D.; Mondal, S.; Bakshi, U.; Saha, K. K.; Saha, S.; Ghosh, A.; Ghosh, A.
abstract: Root exudates play critical roles in rhizosphere microbiome assembly. Nevertheless, the molecular mechanisms by which plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) perceive these signals, adapt to the rhizosphere, and influence native microbial communities remain poorly understood. Here, using maize (Zea mays cv. Early Golden Bantam) and the rhizobacterium Priestia aryabhattai AB211, we took a multi-omics approach combining metabolomics, bacterial transcriptomics and proteomics, and rhizosphere metagenomics to elucidate the mechanism underlying this process. Maize root exudates were enriched in diverse carbon and nitrogen metabolites that promoted bacterial growth and induced extensive molecular reprogramming of pathways involved in nutrient acquisition, chemotaxis, motility, stress adaptation, and plant growth promotion, thereby enhancing rhizosphere competence. In field-conditioned soil, AB211 persisted as a core member of the maize rhizosphere microbiome, promoted early seedling growth, and reshaped microbial community composition and function. Root exudates-primed (RE-primed) AB211 further enhanced the enrichment of microbial functions associated with nutrient cycling, quorum sensing, plant growth promotion, and rhizosphere fitness, highlighting the role of root exudates in modulating the rhizosphere-adaptative potential of beneficial bacteria. These findings establish a mechanistic framework linking root exudates composition with PGPR adaptation and microbiome assembly, providing a foundation for engineering ecologically adapted microbial inoculants to improve crop productivity and sustainable agriculture.

title: Concentration-dependent inhibition of Streptococcus mutans metabolic activity by purified Croton lechleri latex (sangre de grado) in vitro
authors: Rondan Villagra, L. F.; Zevallos Chavez, M.; Franjo Rendulich, J.; Ortega Suni, M. F.; Figueroa Banda, R. A.
abstract: Background. Chlorhexidine is the reference chemical antiplaque agent, but its adverse effects motivate the search for plant-derived alternatives. The proanthocyanidin-rich latex of Croton lechleri (sangre de grado) is a candidate, yet quantitative concentration-response data against Streptococcus mutans are scarce. Methods. In this exploratory in vitro study, ethanol-purified C. lechleri latex was tested at working concentrations of 3-100% v/v (final in-well concentrations 0.6-20% v/v) against S. mutans ATCC 25175 in a 96-well resazurin assay with dual-wavelength reading (570/600 nm) and correction for medium and latex color. Chlorhexidine 1% (0.2% in-well) was the positive control. Each condition was run in technical triplicate within a single experiment. Data were analyzed by one-way ANOVA, Tukey's test with simultaneous 95% confidence intervals (CI) and four-parameter logistic regression. Results. Metabolic activity decreased monotonically with concentration, from 101.3 +/- 1.7% (vehicle) to 54.0 +/- 4.7% (12%), 15.5 +/- 4.0% (50%) and 8.6 +/- 7.7% (100%), compared with 3.1 +/- 2.8% for chlorhexidine (F(7,16) = 160.7, p < 0.001). The lowest concentration that differed from the vehicle was 6% (difference 17.6 percentage points, 95% CI 2.1-33.1). The estimated half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) was 12.3% v/v (95% CI 9.5-15.1). Differences from chlorhexidine at 50% and 100% were not statistically significant, but their confidence intervals were compatible with differences of up to 28 and 21 percentage points, respectively. Conclusions. Purified C. lechleri latex inhibited the metabolic activity of planktonic S. mutans in a concentration-dependent manner. These preliminary findings do not establish equivalence with chlorhexidine and warrant replication in independent experiments with chemically standardized extracts expressed in mg/mL, determination of MIC/MBC and biofilm models.

title: REMAG: recovery of eukaryotic genomes from metagenomic data using non-contrastive self-supervised learning
authors: Gomez-Perez, D.; Raguideau, S.; Warring, S.; James, R.; Hildebrand, F.; Quince, C.
abstract: Metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) are central to exploring microbial communities. Yet, despite the relevance of protists and fungi to diverse ecosystems, eukaryotic MAG recovery lags behind that of prokaryotes. A major bottleneck is that most state-of-the-art binning pipelines exclusively rely on prokaryotic single-copy core gene reference databases and are optimized for smaller genomes. To address this gap, we present REMAG (Recovery of Eukaryotic MAGs), a tool designed to recover high-quality eukaryotic genomes suited for long-read metagenomic data. REMAG uses a fine-tuned HyenaDNA genomic foundation model to efficiently filter eukaryotic contigs. It then employs a dual-encoder Siamese network trained with the non-contrastive Barlow Twins loss to learn a shared embedding space by integrating contig composition and differential coverage. Finally, high-quality bins are extracted using greedy iterative Leiden clustering optimized with eukaryotic single-copy core gene constraints. In benchmarks based on simulated mixed prokaryotic/eukaryotic communities and real datasets of varying sizes and origin, we demonstrate REMAG's ability to recover more near-complete eukaryotic genomes than existing state-of-the-art tools, which often produce highly fragmented eukaryotic bins. REMAG provides an automated eukaryotic binning method that scales effectively with the increasing size and sequencing depth of metagenomic datasets.

title: Calibrated analysis framework for nanopore direct RNA sequencing uncovers cell-specific m6A proportions at conserved sites
authors: Ohnezeit, D.; Loliashvili, E.; Putzel, G.; Verstraten, R.; Silhavy, A. T.; Liu, J.; Nicholson, L. S.; Pironti, A.; Jaffrey, S. R.; Depledge, D. P.; Wilson, A. C.
abstract: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) coupled with Dorado modification-aware basecalling enables mapping of epitranscriptomic modifications including N6-methyladenosine (m6A) at the level of individual RNAs. However, the sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility of this method remain unclear and have only recently begun to be addressed through systematic benchmarking studies. Here, we aimed to establish a best-practice workflow for DRS-based epitranscriptomic analyses. Specifically, we evaluated multiple Dorado versions and models using RNA isolated from primary cells and unmodified in vitro transcribed RNAs. We further utilized an m6A methyltransferase inhibitor as a specificity control. We established that stringent filtering is necessary to reduce the contribution of background and found that Dorado predictions captured an increasing proportion of GLORI sites detected at high m6A/A proportions. Further, by applying DRS to a human primary fibroblast and a HD10.6 neuron dataset, we detected differences in the predicted m6A/A proportions at conserved sites between these datasets. Our study thus presents the first systematic comparison of Dorado and GLORI from the same input RNA and expands characterization of the m6A epitranscriptome to fibroblasts and neurons.

title: Towards standards for analysing structural variants from short-read whole genome sequencing data
authors: Slimmer, J. C.; Jones, J. L.; Reay, W. R.; Burdon, K. P.; Blackburn, N. B.
topics: Antimicrobial Resistance; Long-Read Microbiology; Bioinformatics Tools
abstract: No widely accepted standard exists for analysing structural variants from short-read whole genome sequencing (WGS) data. We use comprehensive SV truth sets (HG002 T2T-Q100, Platinum Pedigree) and long-read sequencing databases (1KGP-ONT, CoLoRS) to benchmark SV breakpoints and sizes at base pair resolution. Using 30X Illumina WGS data, only five of sixteen individual tools tested reliably output deletions, insertions and duplications that perfectly match the truth sets. Ensemble pipelines (e.g. GATK-SV, MOPline, Parliament2), frequently used in population-scale datasets, reduced perfect matching accuracy by up to 98% compared to their highest-performing constituent tools. This inaccuracy propagates into a short-read database (gnomAD-SV) constructed from an ensemble pipeline (GATK-SV) and likely affects other databases (TOPMed, All of Us, Biobank Japan). As a proof-of-concept, we demonstrate an intra-sample merging strategy that generates the highest F1-scores for deletions and insertions on the HG002 sample, recovering more perfect matches than total matches from the best performing ensemble pipeline tested. Common HG002 truth SVs (allele frequency > 1%) showed extremely high concordance for exact matches between our ensemble callset and two orthogonal long-read sequencing databases (CoLoRS, ONT-1KGP). This study provides a vital step towards robust standards for SV analysis, guiding short-read WGS ensemble pipeline development and improving cross-study comparisons.

title: Genus-wide re-speciation of Corynebacterium and genomic characterisation of 87 sinus isolates resolves taxonomic conflicts and identifies four candidate novel species
authors: Burdon, I. A.; Psaltis, J. P.; Vrodos, N. C.; Sung, J.; Durr, L.; Barry, E.; Cooksley, C.; Vreugde, S.; Wormald, P. J.; Psaltis, A. J.
topics: Antimicrobial Resistance; Long-Read Microbiology; Bioinformatics Tools
abstract: Corynebacterium species are common members of the sinonasal microbiome and have shown conflicting associations with sinus health and chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) in genus-level surveys. To better resolve the taxonomy and species-level functions of sinus corynebacteria, we generated complete long-read genome assemblies for 87 isolates, sourced from the middle meatus of 71 patients (51 with CRS, 20 healthy controls). We re-derived species boundaries de novo across the whole genus by average nucleotide identity (ANI), clustering 4,661 quality-filtered genomes retrieved from public databases and delineating higher-order species complexes. Our re-speciation assigned a species to 282 unlabelled corynebacteria, and corrected taxonomy for 266 NCBI accessions. We identified four novel candidate species from our isolate collection, and 39 public genomes fell within these species' boundaries. Whole-genome assignment reclassified 41 of our 87 isolates relative to mass-spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) identification, which only resolved to the species-complex level. Comparison of genome annotation characterised accessory functions that partitioned along species-complex lines, including glycogen and glycan utilisation, fatty-acid biosynthesis, cofactor (biotin and thiamine) auxotrophy, and iron-acquisition systems. Virulence and antimicrobial-resistance determinants were sparse, and the diphtheria toxin gene was universally absent. Acquired antimicrobial resistance was enriched on plasmids, whilst virulence genes were depleted from horizontally transferred compartments. Contrary to its frequent report in sinus microbiome studies, no C. tuberculostearicum genome publicly accessible via NCBI was found to be isolated from the sinonasal tract. Continued genome-level interrogation of Corynebacterium and contribution of sinus-commensals to reference databases will improve species-level understanding of the role of corynebacteria in the sinonasal microbiome.

title: Development of a stable microbial community for the study of plasmid-mediated antimicrobial resistance in a continuous culturing device
authors: Vu, T.-H.; Alonso-Vasquez, T.; Sestini, E.; Masoni, A.; Grabowski, K.; Andrieu, C.; Laganenka, L.; Di Patti, F.; Fondi, M.; Galardini, M.
abstract: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is a major contributor to the spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in microbial communities, particularly through conjugative plasmids. The dynamics of the spread of these plasmids in a susceptible microbial community requires a defined and controllable in vitro system, which is currently lacking from existing laboratory evolution systems. Here we describe the development of TriComm, an engineered microbial community of three strains with complementary amino acid auxotrophies, maintained in continuous culture under real-time optical and fluorescence monitoring. We show that two conjugative plasmids carrying resistance genes (blaOXA-48 and mcr-1) generally rescued TriComm from collapse under antimicrobial treatment, and that this protection was dependent on conjugative transfer. Community composition remained stable across most conditions, including after the AMR plasmid had spread through the population. Through mathematical modeling we predict that modulating both drug efficacy and conjugation rate can lead to the collapse of the community, suggesting potential strategies to limit the spread of AMR via HGT.

title: Microbial persistence beneath temporal restructuring in university wastewater metagenomes
authors: Franco, G.; Anand, A.
abstract: Temporal changes in wastewater microbiomes can reflect shifts in microbial abundance, detectable membership, and genome recovery. We paired genome-resolved and read-based metagenomics to distinguish these signals in 25 spatially pooled university wastewater samples collected during wet and dry periods. The workflow recovered 203 wet-period and 230 dry-period metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). Community composition differed between periods in both MAG-derived presence/absence profiles (Jaccard PERMANOVA, R2 = 0.548, p = 0.001) and read-based relative-abundance profiles (BrayCurtis PERMANOVA, R2 = 0.167, p = 0.001). Greater dry-period read-based richness persisted after rarefaction but disappeared under more stringent abundance thresholds, indicating a substantial contribution from low-abundance detections. Of 57 period-associated core species in the MAG-derived profiles, 14 had exact species-level matches in the read-based dataset. All 14 remained detectable at >=90% prevalence in the opposite period, and 13 had higher relative abundance in the period corresponding to their MAG-based association. Continued species detection therefore accompanied changes in community composition and MAG-based representation. Perfect/Strict CARD/RGI resistance-associated annotations occurred in 94.1% of wet-period and 92.2% of dry-period MAGs and were distributed across shared-core and period-associated taxa. These findings reveal repeated detection of a matched subset of microbial taxa beneath temporal community restructuring, together with widespread resistance-associated genetic potential among recovered genomes. Combining read-based and genome-resolved profiles helps distinguish changes in detectable membership from changes in the genomic characterization available for wastewater surveillance.

title: Resolution of chromosomal structural variation and vanA plasmid dynamics by nanopore-only sequencing across successive waves of a hospital outbreak of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium
authors: Yanagihara, M.; KARINO, M.; Ohtaki, H.; Hanada, H.; Takano, T.; Yamato, M.; Okamoto, S.
abstract: Allele-based typing may incompletely resolve vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) outbreaks in clinical laboratories because it can miss chromosomal structural variation and resistance plasmid dynamics. We evaluated a nanopore-only sequencing workflow in 68 VREfm isolates collected during a single-hospital outbreak predominantly involving Bezdicek multilocus sequence typing (MLST) sequence types (STs) 1162 and 610. Isolates were sequenced on R10.4.1 flow cells, basecalled using Dorado with the super-accurate model, and assembled using Autocycler. Analyses included in silico MLST, core-genome MLST (cgMLST), IS256 insertion-site mapping, whole-chromosome comparison, replicon typing, and complete vanA plasmid sequence comparison. All isolates yielded complete assemblies, and nanopore-derived MLST results matched previous Sanger results.
